Internal Incident Report: Sunder Hill Water Main Burst and Flooding

On the night of 14 March, a 150-millimetre cast-iron water main laid in the 1950s burst beneath the Sunder Hill allotments, sending water down the slope. Corvane Water Authority pressure logs show zone pressure in the Sunder Hill area falling from 4.2 bar to 1.1 bar over roughly 25 minutes. Nine terraced houses on Orchard Steps lost supply. Resident Dalia Finch reported her tap running to a thin trickle before stopping completely, and noted cloudy water for a short period after supply returned. The pressure log records zone pressure back above 3.5 bar by the evening of the same day. A temporary bowser of drinking water was placed at the foot of Orchard Steps during the outage.

Crew leader Anil Ostrowe's team began excavating at the start of the day shift and reached the pipe at a depth of roughly 1.4 metres, then fitted a stainless steel repair clamp over the damaged section. The cause of the failure is disputed. The Authority's repair work order attributes the break to corrosion thinning the pipe wall, while Ostrowe states that ground movement after heavy rain cracked the pipe and that corrosion was not a factor. This should be reconciled before any replacement decision is made.

The flood caused significant damage on the allotments. Allotment warden Greta Pryor reported brown water running on the lower paths, topsoil washed onto the lane below from eleven of thirty-four plots, two polytunnels flattened on the lower terrace, and fourteen plots with crops or structures damaged. The Sunder Hill Allotment Society minute book records nine plots with damaged crops or structures, a discrepancy with the warden's count that needs checking. The shared tool shed stood in a shallow pool but was not damaged. A members' meeting has been called for the following Saturday to discuss clearing the silt.

Sources: Crew leader Anil Ostrowe, Corvane Water Authority repair work order, Corvane Water Authority pressure log, Allotment warden Greta Pryor, Sunder Hill Allotment Society minute book, Resident Dalia Finch
-----

On 9 October at about 4:50 a.m., a 400-millimetre water main beneath the Tolliver Quay processing yard in Vesper Bay split open, flooding the yard and the loading road. The repair job sheet describes the main as cast or ductile iron laid decades earlier and records a repair clamp fitted around the opened section. Water company telemetry shows pressure in the main falling from 5.2 bar to 1.1 bar over roughly six minutes beginning at 4:50 a.m., and a hydrant sensor on the next street recorded pressure reaching zero shortly after the break.

The night watchman, Maren Oduya, heard a loud crack from the yard while on his rounds and then saw water rising around the base of the ice plant. He reported that the yard's tidal sluice gate was open at the time and that some water drained toward the harbour. From the gatehouse he telephoned the water company's emergency line and gave the yard address.

Ines Halloran, the cold-store supervisor, found the cold-store floor drains backing up when she arrived to open the building. Before water reached the building she moved crated stock onto upper racking. Her account puts the peak water depth at the cold-store door at about 15 centimetres, while the gate camera archive suggests about 40 centimetres; this discrepancy requires resolution. Camera timestamps show the first delivery lorry of the day was turned away at the gate because the road was under water.

The foreman's notebook records a crew of five arriving with a pump truck to begin draining the yard, and a ground slump about two metres across above the pipe. Accounts of the time needed to isolate the break differ: the job sheet gives about 70 minutes after arrival, while the notebook gives about 25 minutes. The job sheet lists valves on both sides of the yard closed to isolate the damaged section, and the notebook records that supply to surrounding streets was restored in stages through the afternoon.

Sources: Ines Halloran, cold-store supervisor; Vesper Bay Water Company Repair Job Sheet; Maren Oduya, night watchman; Tolliver Quay Works Foreman's Notebook; Tolliver Quay Gate Camera Archive; Vesper Bay Water Company Pressure Telemetry Record

On 9 October at about 4:50 a.m., a 400-millimetre water main beneath the Tolliver Quay processing yard in Vesper Bay split open, flooding the yard and the loading road. Before water reached the building she moved crated stock onto upper racking. Her account puts the peak water depth at the cold-store door at about 15 centimetres, while the gate camera archive suggests about 40 centimetres; this discrepancy requires resolution. Camera timestamps show the first delivery lorry of the day was turned away at the gate because the road was under water.

The foreman's notebook records a crew of five arriving with a pump truck to begin draining the yard, and a ground slump about two metres across above the pipe. Accounts of the time needed to isolate the break differ: the job sheet gives about 70 minutes after arrival, while the notebook gives about 25 minutes. The job sheet lists valves on both sides of the yard closed to isolate the damaged section, and the notebook records that supply to surrounding streets was restored in stages through the afternoon.

On the night of 14 March, a 150-millimetre cast-iron water main laid in the 1950s burst beneath the Sunder Hill allotments, sending water down the slope. Corvane Water Authority pressure logs show zone pressure in the Sunder Hill area falling from 4.2 bar to 1.1 bar over roughly 25 minutes. Nine terraced houses on Orchard Steps lost supply. Resident Dalia Finch reported her tap running to a thin trickle before stopping completely, and noted cloudy water for a short period after supply returned. The pressure log records zone pressure back above 3.5 bar by the evening of the same day. A temporary bowser of drinking water was placed at the foot of Orchard Steps during the outage.

Crew leader Anil Ostrowe's team began excavating at the start of the day shift and reached the pipe at a depth of roughly 1.4 metres, then fitted a stainless steel repair clamp over the damaged section. The cause of the failure is disputed. The Authority's repair work order attributes the break to corrosion thinning the pipe wall, while Ostrowe states that ground movement after heavy rain cracked the pipe and that corrosion was not a factor. This should be reconciled before any replacement decision is made.

The flood caused significant damage on the allotments. Allotment warden Greta Pryor reported brown water running on the lower paths, topsoil washed onto the lane below from eleven of thirty-four plots, two polytunnels flattened on the lower terrace, and fourteen plots with crops or structures damaged. The Sunder Hill Allotment Society minute book records nine plots with damaged crops or structures, a discrepancy with the warden's count that needs checking. The shared tool shed stood in a shallow pool but was not damaged. A members' meeting has been called for the following Saturday to discuss clearing the silt.

Sources: Crew leader Anil Ostrowe, Corvane Water Authority repair work order, Corvane Water Authority pressure log, Allotment warden Greta Pryor, Sunder Hill Allotment Society minute book, Resident Dalia Finch

**Internal Incident Report: Sunder Hill Water Main Failure**

On the night of 14 March, a 150-millimetre cast-iron water main laid in the 1950s burst beneath the Sunder Hill allotments, sending water down the slope. The Corvane Water Authority pressure log shows zone pressure in the Sunder Hill area falling from 4.2 bar to 1.1 bar over roughly 25 minutes. The supply loss affected nine terraced houses on Orchard Steps. Resident Dalia Finch reported that her tap ran only a thin trickle before stopping completely, and that water was cloudy for a short time after supply returned. The pressure log records zone pressure back above 3.5 bar by the evening of the same day. During the outage, the Authority placed a temporary bowser of drinking water at the foot of Orchard Steps.

On site, crew leader Anil Ostrowe's team began excavating at the start of the day shift and reached the pipe at a depth of roughly 1.4 metres. The crew fitted a stainless steel repair clamp over the damaged section. The cause of the failure is disputed. The Authority's repair work order attributes the break to corrosion that thinned the pipe wall. Crew leader Ostrowe states that ground movement on the slope after heavy rain cracked the pipe and that corrosion was not a factor. This discrepancy should be reconciled before any replacement decision is made.

The flood caused significant damage on the allotments. Allotment warden Greta Pryor found the lower paths running with brown water and reported that eleven of the thirty-four plots had topsoil washed onto the lane below, two polytunnels on the lower terrace were flattened, and fourteen plots had crops or structures damaged. The Sunder Hill Allotment Society minute book records nine plots with damaged crops or structures, which differs from the warden's count and should be checked. The society's shared tool shed stood in a shallow pool but was not damaged. A members' meeting has been called for the following Saturday to discuss clearing the silt.

Sources: Crew leader Anil Ostrowe, Corvane Water Authority repair work order, Corvane Water Authority pressure log, Allotment warden Greta Pryor, Sunder Hill Allotment Society minute book, Resident Dalia Finch
-----

On 9 October, at about 4:50 a.m., a 400-millimetre water main beneath the Tolliver Quay processing yard in Vesper Bay split open, flooding the yard and the loading road. The night watchman, Maren Oduya, heard a loud crack while on his rounds and saw water rising around the base of the ice plant. He telephoned the water company's emergency line from the gatehouse and gave the yard address. Pressure telemetry from the main shows a fall from 5.2 bar to 1.1 bar over roughly six minutes beginning at 4:50 a.m., and a hydrant sensor on the next street recorded pressure reaching zero shortly after the break. Oduya also reported that the tidal sluice gate was open at the time, and some of the water drained toward the harbour.

The repair crew of five arrived with a pump truck and began draining the yard. Accounts differ on how long isolation took. The repair job sheet records about 70 minutes to close the valves on both sides of the yard and isolate the damaged section, while the foreman's notebook records about 25 minutes. A repair clamp was fitted around the opened section, and the foreman noted a hole about two metres across where the ground had slumped above the pipe. Gate camera footage shows water spreading across the loading road toward the quay edge, and the first delivery lorry of the day was turned away because the road was under water.

Inside the cold store, supervisor Ines Halloran found the floor drains backing up when she arrived to open the building. Water at the cold-store door peaked at about 40 centimetres according to the camera archive, although Halloran's own account gives about 15 centimetres. Before the water reached the building, she had moved crated stock onto upper racking to keep it clear. Supply to surrounding streets was restored in stages through the afternoon. The discrepancies in isolation time and door water depth should be reconciled before the report is finalised.

Sources: Ines Halloran, Maren Oduya, Vesper Bay Water Company Repair Job Sheet, Vesper Bay Water Company Pressure Telemetry Record, Tolliver Quay Works Foreman's Notebook, Tolliver Quay Gate Camera Archive
-----

The society's minute book records nine plots with damaged crops or structures, while Greta Pryor's count gives fourteen, so this figure needs reconciling. The fire at the Greywater Marine Supply warehouse on Cormorant Slip, Pellick Sound, began in the net and rope store during the afternoon of 27 August. The smoke detector panel recorded its first alarm from the rear loft zone at 15:42, and that zone stopped transmitting at 15:51, after which no further readings were received. The night watchman, Teodor Absalon, saw grey smoke under the eaves while outside on the quayside and attempted to fight it with a hand extinguisher on the loading door before retreating from the heat. The first fire engine arrived a few minutes after the call was received. Because the warehouse is roughly 90 metres from the nearest hydrant on Sedgewick Parade, crews supplemented the hydrant supply by drawing seawater from the harbour basin with a portable pump. The loft roof collapsed inward during the response and crews withdrew from the upper floor.

Accounts of the time to control differ and must be reconciled in the final review. The harbourmaster stated that the fire was brought under control about 90 minutes after the first engine arrived, while the fire service log records control about 50 minutes after arrival. A light westerly wind carried smoke across the fish market toward the ferry landing. Harbourmaster Idris Colvane ordered two moored trawlers towed away from the adjoining quay wall as a precaution. Absalon reported that four vessels were moved during the fire, a figure that should be checked against harbour records.

The insurance loss assessor, Brenna Oakhallow, found that the sprinkler system covered only the ground floor and not the loft, and estimated the destroyed stock and fittings at roughly 410,000 in local currency. The stock ledger recorded 340 coils of braided polypropylene rope at the last weekly count and showed that 60 new nylon trawl nets had been delivered and shelved four days before the fire. No injuries were recorded among staff, crew, or bystanders.

Incident Summary: Water Main Failure, Chapel Rise Road

On the morning of 22 February, a water main failure on Chapel Rise Road affected three locations: Linden Court, a sheltered housing block of 34 flats; the neighbouring Wystmere Cemetery; and the road itself. The Zone 7 flow meter recorded inflow at roughly three times its overnight baseline before the reading was flagged, and a high-flow alert was raised at 6:12 a.m. The warden at Linden Court recorded loss of running water at about 6:20 a.m. The first customer call reporting low pressure came from a resident at 6:25 a.m., and eleven calls about low pressure or no water were logged between 6:25 and 8:00 a.m. Residents were initially told supply would be restored by evening. The warden arranged for bottled water to be carried to residents unable to manage the stairs.

A Penhallow Water Services crew closed the valves on Chapel Rise Road. The customer call log records the main as fully isolated at 7:05 a.m., and the flow meter shows inflow returning to near baseline after closure. The groundskeeper gave 7:40 a.m. for full isolation. This discrepancy between records should be reconciled during review.

At the cemetery, water ran across the lower burial ground. The groundskeeper, Odile Marchetti, found water running through the lower gate on arrival, and floodwater reached the surface of graves in that area. The number of affected graves is recorded as 14 by the groundskeeper and 22 in the gatehouse visitor book, and this figure needs checking. Floodwater also carried gravel and soil from the road verge onto the central path. The cemetery was closed to visitors from 7:00 a.m. until early afternoon, and a funeral party of about thirty due at 11:00 a.m. was redirected to the upper chapel.

Councillor Rufus Adeyemi-Clay visited the site, stated that the road surface beside the cemetery wall had shown a dip for several weeks, and asked that the old cast-iron pipes along Chapel Rise Road be reviewed.

Sources: Wystmere Sheltered Housing Warden's Diary; Penhallow Water Services Zone 7 Flow Meter Record; Penhallow Water Services Customer Call Log; Odile Marchetti, groundskeeper at Wystmere Cemetery; Wystmere Cemetery Gatehouse Visitor Book; Councillor Rufus Adeyemi-Clay

The water main beneath Garrick Terrace lane in Norrowby failed at about 2:25 p.m. on 17 January, flooding the lock-up garage court and cutting supply to nearby cottages. Pressure on the Garrick Terrace supply line had held steady near 4.6 bar through the morning, then fell to 1.1 bar within six minutes around the time of the burst. The failed section was a 250-millimetre ductile iron main laid beneath the lane. A repair crew reached the site at 2:58 p.m. and began closing valves on both sides of the break. The repair job sheet records that water stopped flowing from the broken main at about 3:20 p.m., although a separate account places that point at about 3:45 p.m. This discrepancy should be reconciled against the timing data. The crew cut out a damaged section of pipe about two metres long and fitted a replacement sleeve.

The lane camera shows water reaching the garage doors at the lower end of the court about ten minutes after the first surfacing. A van was recorded backing out of the court as water spread across the gravel, and gravel and silt were carried about thirty metres down the lane, settling against the court gate. Several tenants had moved cars and stored paint tins out of the lower garages before the water arrived there. The number of affected units is inconsistent across sources: the camera archive indicates seven lock-up garages had water inside at the peak of flooding, while the caretaker's notebook records eleven. This figure requires reconciliation before the report is finalised. Caretaker Wilfrid Aspinmoor heard a loud thump from the lane, then saw water bubbling up through the gravel beside the third garage. He telephoned the water company from the caretaker's hut and logged the call.

Residents of the nearby cottages lost supply. Hester Pimbrell reported that her kitchen tap was running only a thin trickle shortly after the water began flooding the lane, and that evening she collected water from a tanker parked at the end of the lane. The pressure record shows supply restored to the Garrick Terrace line at 8:40 p.m. The lane surface was left with a shallow trench filled with temporary stone following the repair, and permanent reinstatement remains outstanding.

Sources: Cottager Hester Pimbrell's statement; Norrowby Water Company Pressure Telemetry Record; Norrowby Water Company Repair Job Sheet; Garrick Terrace Lane Camera Archive; Lock-up caretaker Wilfrid Aspinmoor's notebook

At 15:42 on 27 August, the smoke detector panel in the rear loft zone of the Greywater Marine Supply warehouse on Cormorant Slip, Pellick Sound, recorded its first alarm. The panel stopped transmitting from that zone at 15:51, and no further readings were received. A fire in the net and rope store was reported that afternoon. The first fire engine reached Cormorant Slip a few minutes after the call was received. The warehouse sits at the end of the slip, roughly 90 metres from the nearest hydrant on Sedgewick Parade, so firefighters drew seawater from the harbor basin with a portable pump to supplement the hydrant supply. Night watchman Teodor Absalon, on the quayside, observed grey smoke under the eaves, used a hand extinguisher on the loading door, and withdrew when the heat became too intense. Harbourmaster Idris Colvane ordered two moored trawlers towed away from the adjoining quay wall as a precaution, since a light westerly wind carried smoke across the fish market toward the ferry landing. During the response the loft roof collapsed inward and crews withdrew from the upper floor. The fire was brought under control about 90 minutes after the first engine arrived. No injuries were recorded among staff, crew, or bystanders. The insurance loss assessor, Brenna Oakhallow, found that the sprinkler system covered only the ground floor and not the loft, and estimated the destroyed stock and fittings at roughly 410,000 in local currency. The stock ledger shows that 60 new nylon trawl nets were received and shelved four days before the fire, and the last weekly count listed 340 coils of braided polypropylene rope in the store.

Sources: Pellick Sound Fire Service incident log, Night watchman Teodor Absalon, Harbourmaster Idris Colvane, Insurance loss assessor Brenna Oakhallow, Greywater Marine Supply stock ledger, Smoke detector panel at Greywater Marine Supply

Inspectors found the underpass drainage gullies partly blocked with packed leaf litter the following morning and noted slight sinking of the road surface near the northern kerb beside the burst. Crew members later identified a lengthwise split about 90 centimetres long in the pipe wall.

The underpass depth marker camera recorded water covering the lowest painted gauge band at 6:22 p.m. The number of stranded vehicles at the peak of flooding differs between sources, with nine given in bus driver Anselm Trevenna's statement and six in the camera record. Council highways staff closed both ends of the underpass with barriers. Bus driver Anselm Trevenna halted his service at the southern entrance as water rose across the road ahead of him, and stated that the water appeared clear rather than muddy when he first saw it. Trevenna's statement counts nine vehicles stranded at peak flooding, while the camera record shows six. This discrepancy should be resolved during review.

Crew leader Dorothea Quillfeather arrived with two fitters and a tanker-mounted pump and found a lengthwise split approximately 90 centimetres long in the pipe wall. Her notes indicate that the main split first and the roadside gully overflowed afterward. The highways inspection sheet records that the gullies were partly blocked with packed leaf litter when inspected the following morning, which bears on how drainage performed during the event. Inspectors also observed slight sinking of the road surface near the northern kerb beside the burst. Water entering the corner bakery on Pilchard Lane reached the shop floor but did not rise above the lowest shelf of the display counter.

The camera record shows the water level falling after the pump arrived, and the pressure record shows slow partial recovery beginning once the damaged section was isolated.

This sequence remains unresolved and should be confirmed before any conclusions are drawn. The following morning, inspectors found the underpass gullies partly blocked with packed leaf litter and a patch of road surface near the northern kerb slightly sunk beside the burst. Council highways staff placed road-closed barriers at both ends of the underpass.

Bus driver Anselm Trevenna stopped his service at the southern mouth of the underpass when water began rising across the road ahead, and he reported that the water appeared clear rather than muddy when first seen. The camera record and the driver's statement differ on the number of vehicles stranded at peak flooding, with six recorded on camera and nine in the driver's statement. Water entering the corner bakery on Pilchard Lane reached the shop floor but did not rise above the lowest shelf of the display counter. The camera record shows the water level falling after the pump arrived, and the pressure record shows a slow partial recovery beginning after the damaged section was isolated.

A chemical spill occurred in the basement supply store of Tovane University Hospital at about 2:15 p.m. on a Thursday in early October. Vapor readings dropped below 10 parts per million at 3:32 p.m. The laundry level remained closed for about 90 minutes, delaying clean linen deliveries to the surgical wing. No patient areas were affected, and no one was sent to the emergency department.

The pallet had been delivered that morning by an outside supplier and had not been rewrapped. Forklift operator Desmond Okafor was moving a pallet of four 55-gallon drums from the loading bay to a storage rack at the time, and he reported no mechanical problems during his shift. The accounts of how the drum was punctured differ. The Safety Office report attributes the puncture to the protruding pallet board striking the drum as the stack was lifted, while Okafor attributed it to a forklift fork tine being driven into the drum when the stack was set down. The operations team should verify both accounts before finalizing the cause.

Sources: Tovane University Hospital Facilities Log, Tovane Hospital Safety Office Incident Report, Basement Level 2 Vapor Monitor, Imogen Harstad, linen services supervisor, Desmond Okafor, forklift operator

The cause and the discrepancy in the volume released should be resolved before the review is finalized.

Estimates of the volume that reached the Wimbrel Ditch differ. The inspector estimated about 300 liters, while the foreman's statement gave about 900 liters. A conductivity probe located 40 meters downstream of the grate rose from 780 to 2,400 microsiemens per centimeter, with the rise beginning at 10:31 a.m., and readings returned below 1,000 microsiemens per centimeter by early evening. The inspector also noted dried residue on the outer rim of the vent pipe.

The accounts also disagree on cause. The foreman attributed the overflow solely to a partly blocked vent pipe, while the inspector attributed it solely to the level transmitter under-reading, which may have led the driver to continue pumping past capacity. The driver remained beside the truck's pump controls for the entire delivery. This review should reconcile the conflicting volume and cause accounts before corrective actions are finalized.

Sources: Harbor Soil Board Inspector Dov Tillerman's report; Saltreach Cranberry Growers Shed Tank Level Transmitter Record; Foreman Pilar Hendrickwood's statement; Marsh Ditch Conductivity Probe Record; Saltreach Growers Delivery Ticket

The Plainsman Cooperative siding in Corliss Junction experienced a release of ammonium thiosulfate solution from a rail tank car at approximately 6:40 a.m. on a Tuesday in late April. The car had arrived two days earlier from the regional terminal carrying roughly 28,000 gallons of the solution. Yard supervisor Tobias Wrenfield identified a wet sheen spreading beneath the car at the start of his shift, and feed mill worker Dagny Ferreira reported a sharp sulfurous odor in the loading bay before any evacuation request was issued. Dispatcher Renata Oyelaran received Wrenfield's call and dispatched the first engine company to the siding.

Responders moved quickly to contain the release. Eleven feed mill employees were evacuated from the mill building, and workers at the grain elevator across the road were directed upwind to the scale house. Light southwesterly winds carried the odor toward the feed mill rather than the town's homes. Firefighters established a perimeter of about 150 meters around the siding and placed absorbent booms across the roadside ditch to keep liquid out of Dunmore Creek. The valve pressure logger recorded a drop from 31 psi to 19 psi over eleven minutes, and the tank car reached zero gauge internal pressure at 7:52 a.m.

Environmental health staff sampled ditch water at three locations and found elevated sulfur compounds at the two sites closest to the siding, prompting a recommendation to excavate about 40 meters of ditch soil. Ferreira and one coworker reported eye irritation and were evaluated by paramedics at the mill. A transfer crew later pumped the remaining contents into a replacement car, a process that continued through the afternoon. The fire department log lists the siding as cleared for normal rail traffic the following morning.

The sources disagree on the cause. Wrenfield attributed the leak solely to a failed bottom outlet valve gasket, while the environmental health field report attributed it solely to a dome-side unloading connection left loose after the previous inspection. The operations team should resolve this conflict before closing the review.

Sources: Corliss Junction Fire Department incident log, Hallett County Environmental Health field report, Tobias Wrenfield, Renata Oyelaran, Dagny Ferreira, Tank car valve pressure logger
-----

**Incident Report: Fertilizer Concentrate Tank Overflow, Saltreach Cranberry Growers Shed, Wimbrel Flats**

On a Monday morning in mid-March, at approximately 10:10 a.m., a 9,000-liter fertilizer concentrate tank overflowed at the Saltreach Cranberry Growers shed in Wimbrel Flats. The tank was being filled from a delivery truck through a hose connected to a fill port on its side. The delivery ticket lists 6,500 liters of liquid fertilizer concentrate as the quantity loaded. Foreman Pilar Hendrickwood observed liquid running down the outside of the tank and across the apron, and she shut the supply valve by hand after reaching the fill port. The driver remained beside the truck's pump controls throughout the delivery.

The tank's overflow vent pipe discharges at the top of the tank wall, about 3 meters above the apron. The inspector noted dried residue on the outer rim of the vent pipe. The apron slopes toward a drain grate that leads to the Wimbrel Ditch. Workers laid absorbent sand socks across the apron in front of the grate, and the inspector recorded that the socks held most of the spilled solution. The inspector estimated that about 300 liters passed through the grate into the ditch, while Hendrickwood estimated about 900 liters. This discrepancy should be reconciled in the final review.

Monitoring data show the effect on the ditch. The tank level transmitter recorded its highest reading at 10:07 a.m. and logs once per minute. The conductivity probe 40 meters downstream of the grate rose from 780 to 2,400 microsiemens per centimeter, beginning to climb at 10:31 a.m. The reading had returned below 1,000 microsiemens per centimeter by early evening.

Sources: Harbor Soil Board Inspector Dov Tillerman's report; Saltreach Cranberry Growers Shed Tank Level Transmitter Record; Foreman Pilar Hendrickwood's statement; Marsh Ditch Conductivity Probe Record; Saltreach Growers Delivery Ticket
-----

On a Tuesday in late April, at approximately 6:40 a.m., a release of ammonium thiosulfate solution was discovered at the Plainsman Cooperative siding in Corliss Junction. Yard supervisor Tobias Wrenfield identified a wet sheen spreading beneath the car at the start of his shift, and feed mill worker Dagny Ferreira reported a sharp sulfurous odor in the loading bay before any evacuation request was issued. Dispatcher Renata Oyelaran received Wrenfield's call and dispatched the first engine company to the siding.

Responders moved quickly to contain the release. Eleven feed mill employees were evacuated from the mill building, and workers at the grain elevator across the road were directed upwind to the scale house. Light southwesterly winds carried the odor toward the feed mill rather than the town's homes. Firefighters established a perimeter of about 150 meters around the siding and placed absorbent booms across the roadside ditch to keep liquid out of Dunmore Creek. The valve pressure logger recorded a drop from 31 psi to 19 psi over eleven minutes, and the tank car reached zero gauge internal pressure at 7:52 a.m.

Environmental health staff sampled ditch water at three locations and found elevated sulfur compounds at the two sites closest to the siding, prompting a recommendation to excavate about 40 meters of ditch soil. Ferreira and one coworker reported eye irritation and were evaluated by paramedics at the mill. A transfer crew later pumped the remaining contents into a replacement car, a process that continued through the afternoon. The fire department log lists the siding as cleared for normal rail traffic the following morning.

The sources disagree on the cause. Wrenfield attributed the leak solely to a failed bottom outlet valve gasket, while the environmental health field report attributed it solely to a dome-side unloading connection left loose after the previous inspection. The operations team should resolve this conflict before closing the review.

Sources: Corliss Junction Fire Department incident log, Hallett County Environmental Health field report, Tobias Wrenfield, Renata Oyelaran, Dagny Ferreira, Tank car valve pressure logger

Environmental health staff sampled ditch water at three locations and found elevated sulfur compounds at the two points nearest the siding, leading to advice to excavate roughly 40 meters of ditch soil. Wrenfield attributes the leak solely to a degraded and failed bottom outlet valve gasket, while the county field report attributes it solely to a dome-side unloading connection left loose after the previous inspection. Eleven employees were initially instructed to evacuate the mill building, though a later account from Ferreira places the number at fourteen. Ferreira and one coworker reported eye irritation and were evaluated by paramedics on site.

The valve pressure logger recorded a decline from 31 psi to 19 psi over eleven minutes, with internal pressure reaching zero gauge at 7:52 a.m. Environmental health staff sampled ditch water at three locations, found elevated sulfur compounds at the two points nearest the siding, and recommended excavation of ditch soil along an approximately 40-meter stretch.

Accounts of the cause conflict. The yard supervisor attributes the release solely to a degraded bottom outlet valve gasket, while the county environmental health report attributes it solely to a dome-side unloading connection left loose after the previous inspection. A transfer crew pumped the remaining contents into a replacement car through the afternoon. The fire department log records the siding as cleared for normal rail traffic the following morning.

The leak occurred at the Plainsman Cooperative siding in Corliss Junction at approximately 6:40 a.m. on a Tuesday in late April. Yard supervisor Tobias Wrenfield identified a wet sheen spreading beneath the car while walking the siding at the start of his shift and called dispatch. Feed mill worker Dagny Ferreira reported a sharp sulfurous odor in the loading bay before any evacuation request was issued. Dispatcher Renata Oyelaran relayed the call and sent the first engine company to the siding.

Responders established a perimeter of about 150 meters. Fourteen feed mill employees were evacuated from the mill building, and workers at the grain elevator across the road were moved upwind to the scale house. Light southwesterly winds carried the odor toward the feed mill rather than the town's homes. Firefighters placed absorbent booms across the roadside ditch to prevent the liquid from reaching Dunmore Creek. Ferreira and one coworker reported eye irritation and were evaluated by paramedics on site.

The valve pressure logger recorded internal pressure falling from 31 psi to 19 psi over eleven minutes, reaching zero gauge at 7:52 a.m. Environmental health staff sampled ditch water at three locations and found elevated sulfur compounds at the two sites nearest the siding. The siding was logged as cleared for normal rail traffic the following morning.

The cause of the leak is disputed in the source material. Wrenfield attributed it solely to a degraded and failed bottom outlet valve gasket, while the county environmental health field report attributed it solely to a dome-side unloading connection left loose after the previous inspection. This discrepancy must be resolved before corrective actions are finalized.

Sources: Corliss Junction Fire Department incident log, Hallett County Environmental Health field report, Plainsman Co-op yard supervisor Tobias Wrenfield, Dispatcher Renata Oyelaran, Feed mill worker Dagny Ferreira, Tank car valve pressure logger

The leak was discovered at the Plainsman Cooperative siding in Corliss Junction at approximately 6:40 a.m. on a Tuesday in late April. The affected tank car had arrived from the regional terminal two days earlier and contained roughly 28,000 gallons of ammonium thiosulfate solution. Yard supervisor Tobias Wrenfield observed a wet sheen spreading beneath the car during his shift-start walk of the siding and notified dispatch. Dispatcher Renata Oyelaran relayed the calls and dispatched the first engine company to the siding.

Responders established a perimeter of approximately 150 meters. Fourteen feed mill employees were evacuated from the mill building, and workers at the grain elevator across the road were moved upwind to the scale house. Light southwesterly winds carried the odor toward the feed mill rather than the town's homes. Firefighters placed absorbent booms across the roadside ditch to keep the liquid from reaching Dunmore Creek. Ferreira and one coworker reported eye irritation and were evaluated by paramedics on site.

The valve pressure logger recorded internal pressure falling from 31 psi to 19 psi over eleven minutes, reaching zero gauge at 7:52 a.m. Environmental health staff sampled ditch water at three locations and found elevated sulfur compounds at the two sites nearest the siding, and they recommended excavating about 40 meters of ditch soil. A transfer crew then moved the remaining contents into a replacement car, a process that continued through the afternoon. The siding was cleared for normal rail traffic the following morning.

The cause of the leak remains disputed. Wrenfield attributed it solely to a degraded and failed bottom outlet valve gasket, while the county environmental health field report attributed it solely to a dome-side unloading connection left loose after the previous inspection. This discrepancy must be resolved before corrective actions are finalized.

Sources: Corliss Junction Fire Department incident log, Hallett County Environmental Health field report, Tobias Wrenfield, Renata Oyelaran, Dagny Ferreira, Tank car valve pressure logger

On the Thursday in early October when this incident occurred, at approximately 2:15 p.m., a drum of alkaline floor-stripper concentrate containing ethanolamine was punctured in the basement supply store at Tovane University Hospital, releasing about 30 gallons onto the concrete floor before the drum was upended and sealed. The drum was one of four 55-gallon drums on a pallet being moved by forklift operator Desmond Okafor from the loading bay to a storage rack. Okafor reported no mechanical problems with his forklift during the shift. The cause of the puncture remains disputed. The Facilities Log and Okafor's statement attribute it to a fork tine striking the drum as the stack was set down, while the Safety Office report attributes it to a protruding pallet board striking the drum during lifting. The pallet had been delivered that morning by an outside supplier and had not been rewrapped.

Linen services supervisor Imogen Harstad noticed a sharp, fishy odor in the linen sorting room shortly before the Basement Level 2 vapor monitor sounded its local horn at 2:19 p.m., when it registered an amine reading of 14 parts per million against an alarm threshold of 10. Harstad directed her crew to exit through the east stairwell and close the fire door. The supply store ventilation unit was switched to full exhaust at 2:24 p.m. The floor drain was found plugged with a rubber mat before the spill reached it. A two-person hospital spill team in chemical suits began absorbing the liquid with granular pads at 2:41 p.m. and sealed the contaminated absorbent into six lined containers for removal by a licensed waste contractor. Readings fell below 10 parts per million at 3:32 p.m.

The laundry level remained closed for roughly 90 minutes to three hours, delaying clean linen deliveries to the surgical wing. No patient areas were affected, and no personnel were transported to the emergency department as a result of the incident.

Sources: Tovane University Hospital Facilities Log, Tovane Hospital Safety Office Incident Report, Basement Level 2 Vapor Monitor, Imogen Harstad, Desmond Okafor
-----

The incident began at about 4:25 a.m. on a Wednesday in early December, when a 1,000-liter tote of liquid drain cleaner cracked at Door 6 of the cold-chain dock at Pennick Dairy Distribution in Thistlebeck and began leaking onto the floor. The tote had been delivered the previous afternoon for the plant's sanitation contractor and was staged on a wooden pallet near the door. Dock lead Marisol Teague completed a walkthrough at 3:50 a.m. and noted nothing unusual. Responders reached the dock at about 4:46 a.m. according to the fire service record, or 4:55 a.m. according to the dock door log, and a Brannoch Regional Fire Service engine was dispatched. Absorbent socks were placed around the nearest floor drain to keep solution out of the sanitary sewer line, and Doors 5, 6, and 7 were closed while the remaining liquid was pumped into a sealed container.

A refrigerated trailer had backed into the bay at Door 6 that morning. Its driver, Gideon Harkness, had been standing beside the rear doors and was moved to the break room, with no skin contact reported. The trailer held yogurt in its rear section, and its doors were closed before liquid reached the loading plate. Door 7 reopened for trailers at 8:05 a.m., while Door 6 remained closed for washdown. The fire service logged the scene as cleared at 7:58 a.m.

The Meridian Cell Network lost service across Dornach Vale on a Saturday in March, beginning at 9:14 a.m., when the Tessaly Cell Site Alarm Monitor recorded a loss-of-signal alarm from the Hollin Rise mast. The monitor also showed the mast's battery backup unit switching on at 9:15 a.m. when mains input dropped, and later logged the backup battery voltage falling to its cutoff level, after which the site went fully dark. The Hollin Rise mast serves roughly 2,300 residents of Dornach Vale and the surrounding farms, so the outage affected a wide area.

The Meridian operations log records that a high-priority fault ticket was opened for the Hollin Rise site. Pell Hartnoll, a Meridian field technician, was dispatched from the Meridian depot in Greaves Cross, about 25 kilometres away. Hartnoll reached the mast compound after driving a farm track that was muddy from overnight rain. He found the cabinet door closed and its lock intact. He replaced a power distribution module in the cabinet and restarted the radio equipment. The operations log records service being restored at 12:40 p.m. following the restart, and the Hollin Rise mast was confirmed back on air at 1:25 p.m.

The impact on local trade was significant. The stallholders' notebook records that the Saturday market opened at 9:00 a.m. with about 30 stalls trading, and that several traders gave customers handwritten receipts and accepted cash only until card readers worked again. Eleven stalls were taking card payments again by the end of the market day, rising to seventeen according to the account of Ines Varga, owner of the Dornach Vale Pharmacy on Fenner Street. Varga could not process card payments and asked customers to pay in cash or return later, and she kept a handwritten list of prescription customers whose payments were deferred until service returned.

Sources: Dornach Vale Market Hall Stallholders' Notebook; Ines Varga, Dornach Vale Pharmacy owner; Meridian Cell Network Operations Log; Tessaly Cell Site Alarm Monitor; Pell Hartnoll, Meridian field technician
-----

Teague's statement attributes it to a forklift tine striking the lower wall during positioning, while Strickland's field report attributes it to cold air from the open door making the aging plastic brittle, with no impact involved. Confirming the cause will require inspecting the tote and interviewing the forklift operator.

A refrigerated trailer had backed into the bay at Door 6 that morning. Its driver, Gideon Harkness, had been standing beside the rear doors and was moved to the break room. No skin contact was reported. His statement notes that the trailer held pallets of yogurt and that its doors were closed before liquid reached the loading plate. First responders reached the dock between 4:46 and 4:55 a.m., and the fire service logged the scene as cleared at 7:58 a.m. Responders placed absorbent socks around the nearest floor drain to keep solution out of the sanitary sewer line, closed Doors 5, 6, and 7, and pumped the remaining liquid into a sealed container. Door 7 reopened for trailers at 8:05 a.m., and Door 6 remains closed for washdown.

The parish clerk's log gives a different sequence, recording that barriers went up at 11:25, before the formal notice was issued, and that stallholders on the far bank were informed of the closure by hand-delivered note. Tennick had last inspected the underside eleven months earlier. The strain monitor on the eastern bearing logged a sharp spike at 08:52 and, between 08:30 and 11:30, recorded a peak of 412 microstrain against a normal daily range below 150. Battery voltage remained within its normal band throughout the morning. Earlier that morning, drover Bram Keswick moved a flock of sheep across the bridge toward the market pens, travelling in loose groups rather than as a single body. The parish clerk also noted that a grain merchant's delivery lorry crossed shortly before the market opened, and logged the river level as ordinary for the season. Tennick attributed the crack to long-term fatigue of the aged support and judged it unrelated to that morning's traffic. Keswick disputed this, maintaining that the lorry's weight while his flock was on the bridge caused the crack rather than age. Separately, the Marlow Ferry operator, two kilometres downstream, ran an extra service between 12:15 and 16:00 carrying 63 foot passengers stranded by the closure. Temperature conditions require attention. The cold room data logger recorded a steady 3.5 degrees Celsius for most of the week but registered a spike to 9.2 degrees Celsius on the night of Thursday 12 June. Separately, the market provides no refrigeration, the stall uses open-sided canopies near the lake shore, and Ms. Quenby displays packs on crushed ice in insulated boxes.

Dr. Halvard Teague, the county environmental health officer, visited the smokehouse on Saturday afternoon, ordered swabs of the slicing table, brine tanks, and processing room drain, and issued a stop-sale order covering all smoked fish products. **Internal Incident Report: Teller Bridge Closure, Nettlefold**

On Thursday, the Teller Bridge at Nettlefold was closed to all traffic at 11:40 following the discovery of a crack approximately 14 centimetres long in the eastern bearing support. The crack was identified by county bridge inspector Orla Tennick during a scheduled underside walk-through. Her previous inspection of the underside had taken place eleven months earlier. Before the closure, the posted weight limit was 7.5 tonnes. Halden County Roads records state that two road crew members placed barriers at both approaches and posted a hand-lettered sign at the market end. The parish clerk's log, however, records the barriers going up at 11:25, before the formal notice was issued. The sequence of events on the morning must be reconciled before the report is finalised.

The strain monitor on the eastern bearing recorded a sharp spike at 08:52 and a peak of 412 microstrain between 08:30 and 11:30, against a normal daily range below 150. Battery voltage remained within its normal band throughout, so the readings do not appear to reflect an instrument fault. Witness accounts place several events within the same window. Drover Bram Keswick moved a flock across the bridge earlier that morning, travelling in loose groups on the way to the Nettlefold market pens. A grain merchant's delivery lorry crossed shortly before the market opened. The river level was ordinary for the season.

Causation remains disputed. Keswick maintains that the crack resulted from the lorry's weight crossing while his flock was on the bridge. Tennick attributes the crack to long-term fatigue in the aged support, unrelated to that morning's traffic. The monitor data alone does not resolve the question, so the review should weigh the timing of the spike against the recorded traffic and the inspection history.

The closure had significant operational impact. The Marlow Ferry operator, two kilometres downstream, ran an additional service carrying 63 foot passengers between 12:15 and 16:00. Stallholders on the far bank were informed of the closure by hand-delivered note.

Sources: Halden County Roads Closure Notice, Teller Bridge Strain Monitor, Drover Bram Keswick, Marlow Ferry Crossing Ledger, Nettlefold Parish Clerk's Log, Inspector Orla Tennick

Estimates of how many people were on the deck when the slow-down was first signalled differ. Warden Leofric Maddox's statement puts the figure at about 340, while race marshal Tamsin Orrelby's notebook puts it at about 260. Maddox also stated that the footbridge carries a posted limit of 300 people on the deck at one time, so both estimates indicate the limit was exceeded. Orrelby observed the handrails visibly swaying while runners crossed in a dense group, and noted that several runners grabbed the handrails and some stopped near the first tower.

Maddox walked onto the deck and instructed runners to slow to a walk and spread out. He reported that no one was injured and that the deck was cleared on foot toward the eastern bank. Both gates were locked, with the Closure Log recording 10:22 and Maddox's statement recording 10:36. This discrepancy should be reconciled. Incident involved Listeria monocytogenes in vacuum-packed smoked trout from Quenby Smokehouse, lot QT-0611, sold at the Wickerby Lakeside Market on Saturday 14 June. The lot was smoked and packed on Wednesday 11 June, with a production log listing 184 packs in total. On 14 June the Brindlemoor Public Health Laboratory confirmed Listeria monocytogenes in a positive sample from an unopened 250-gram pack bearing lot code QT-0611, with the detected level reported above 100 colony-forming units per gram. The isolate was grown on selective agar following a 48-hour enrichment.

Sales records conflict on the number of affected packs sold at the market stall that morning. The stall owner reported exactly 42 packs sold, while the market manager reported exactly 67. These figures must be reconciled before any customer notification is finalized. The market manager estimated that about 60 shoppers stopped at the stall during the morning.

Cold-chain conditions require review. The smokehouse cold-room data logger held a steady 3.5 degrees Celsius for most of the week but spiked to 9.2 degrees Celsius on the night of Thursday 12 June. At the market, packs were displayed on crushed ice in insulated boxes. The market does not provide refrigeration, and stalls operate under open-sided canopies near the lake shore.

County environmental health officer Dr. Halvard Teague visited the smokehouse on Saturday afternoon, ordered swabs of the slicing table, brine tanks, and processing room drain, and issued a stop-sale order covering all smoked fish products. The order reached the market stall at about 1:10 p.m. according to the health officer and about 1:45 p.m. according to the market manager. The market manager stopped trout sales within minutes of the call. The owner notified regular customers by phone and posted a notice on the smokehouse door that evening.

Incident Report: Skarrowby Tow Bridge Closure, Early June

On a Wednesday afternoon in early June, the Skarrowby Tow Bridge was closed to all road and pedestrian traffic after a barge struck the bridge's timber fender and the northern approach span was left out of line. The bridge carries a single lane of traffic with a footway on its western side. The barge involved, the Marigold Drift, was carrying 40 tonnes of gravel and was travelling downstream toward the bridge when it touched the fender. According to barge master Iolanthe Quillfeather, the vessel was moving at walking pace, as required near the bridge, and conditions included a light current and clear visibility. Her account and the lock keeper's notebook record different times of first contact, and this discrepancy has not yet been reconciled. Following the contact, the Marigold Drift was moored at the Skarrowby lower landing, where the crew checked the hull for damage.

Lock keeper Wilfrid Marchbanks heard a loud splintering noise from the fender and walked onto the bridge to inspect the northern approach. He observed a gap of roughly two fingers' width between the planking of the northern approach and the main deck, and he closed the swing gates at the southern end by hand. Deck level survey records show the northern approach span sat 4 millimetres lower in the two hours before impact, which is within normal seasonal movement. The largest drop in the first hour after impact is reported differently across sources, with one reading of 31 millimetres and another of about 55 millimetres, and this should be resolved before any structural conclusions are drawn. A bus dispatch record also notes a driver reporting a bump at the northern approach on the run before the closure. The number 14 route has since been diverted over the Harcombe road crossing, adding about 9 kilometres to each round trip. The bridge will remain closed until a structural engineer has assessed the northern approach span.

Sources: Skarrowby Canal Trust Closure Notice, Barge master Iolanthe Quillfeather's statement, Skarrowby Tow Bridge Deck Level Survey Record, Lock keeper Wilfrid Marchbanks's notebook, Skarrowby Parish Bus Service Dispatch Record

Internal Incident Report: Listeria monocytogenes Detection in Vacuum-Packed Smoked Trout, Lot QT-0611

This report concerns vacuum-packed smoked trout produced by Quenby Smokehouse. Lot QT-0611 was smoked and packed on Wednesday 11 June, according to the production log, which lists 184 packs in the lot. On Saturday 14 June, the Brindlemoor Public Health Laboratory confirmed Listeria monocytogenes in an unopened 250-gram pack bearing lot code QT-0611, with the detected level reported as above 100 colony-forming units per gram. The isolate was grown on selective agar following a 48-hour enrichment. The product had been sold at the Wickerby Lakeside Market that morning, where about 60 shoppers reportedly stopped at the stall.

The cold room data logger at the smokehouse recorded a steady 3.5 degrees Celsius for most of the week but also registered a spike to 9.2 degrees Celsius on the night of Thursday 12 June. The production log states that brine tanks are emptied and sanitized every Monday. The market does not provide refrigeration for vendors, and stalls sit under open-sided canopies near the lake shore. During market hours, the smokehouse owner displays packs on crushed ice in insulated boxes.

The county environmental health officer visited the smokehouse on Saturday afternoon, ordered swabs of the slicing table, brine tanks, and processing room drain, and issued a stop-sale order covering all smoked fish products. The market manager stopped trout sales at the stall within minutes of receiving the stop-sale call. The owner notified regular customers by phone and by a notice posted at the smokehouse door on Saturday evening.

Discrepancies requiring verification: the time the stop-sale order reached the market stall is recorded as about 1:45 p.m. by the market manager and about 1:10 p.m. in the county environmental health officer's account. The number of packs sold from lot QT-0611 at the stall on 14 June is reported as 42 by the smokehouse owner and as 67 by the market manager. Neither discrepancy has been resolved, and both should be verified before the figures are relied upon.

Sources: Marisol Quenby, owner of Quenby Smokehouse; Quenby Smokehouse production log; Tobias Ferrant, market manager at Wickerby Lakeside Market; Dr. Halvard Teague, county environmental health officer; Brindlemoor Public Health Laboratory report; Cold-room temperature data logger at Quenby Smokehouse

The Merrowdyke Lift Bridge incident began during a scheduled raise of the span for the barge Lodestar at the start of bridge keeper Ansel Throckmorton's shift. Throckmorton's logbook records the lift as halted at 07:52 with the span at its maximum height, with traffic signals on both approaches switched to red and barrier arms lowered. The span encoder record logs the halt at 07:58, with the deck having risen to a maximum of 9.6 metres above the closed position. This six-minute discrepancy between the logbook and the encoder must be reconciled as part of the review. Throckmorton noticed broken wire strands hanging from the northwest counterweight cable and stopped the lift before it could proceed further.

Tug master Philippa Kestenholme reported that the Lodestar was carrying about 180 tonnes of gravel bound for the Sellick Weir depot. She held the vessel and its two barges against the downstream mooring dolphins while the span was lowered, which the encoder indicates occurred at roughly one-third of normal speed. The Lodestar was permitted to pass beneath the span only after the Board arranged a lower-clearance transit the following day.

Cable inspector Ottoline Frayne counted 31 broken outer wires along a two-metre stretch of the northwest cable. She found the other three counterweight cables intact but recommended they be checked before any reopening. The Navigation Board closed the bridge to all road traffic and pedestrians on the Monday in mid-November, stating it would remain shut until all four cables were examined and the northwest cable replaced. The bridge is a Grade II structure with a rated lifting cycle of roughly 40 raises per month.

Operational impacts included stopped vehicles at the south barrier, with nine vehicles held in one count and fourteen in another once the span was fully seated, and two buses held at the Dyke Street stop while dispatchers confirmed the new route. The number 14 service now runs over the signed diversion via Quarry Road and the Sellick Weir crossing, adding about 11 kilometres to each round trip.

Sources: Bridge keeper Ansel Throckmorton's logbook, Merrowdyke Navigation Board Closure Notice, Tug master Philippa Kestenholme's statement, Merrowdyke Parish Bus Service Dispatch Record, Merrowdyke Lift Bridge Span Height Encoder Record, Cable inspector Ottoline Frayne's report

The Skarrowby Tow Bridge was closed to all road and pedestrian traffic on a Wednesday afternoon in early June after the barge Marigold Drift, carrying 40 tonnes of gravel and travelling downstream at walking pace, made contact with the bridge's timber fender. The barge master, Iolanthe Quillfeather, recorded first contact at 14:21, while the lock keeper's notebook records it at 14:12. This discrepancy must be resolved against the lock log during the review. Quillfeather reported a light current and clear visibility at the time. The Marigold Drift was subsequently moored at the Skarrowby lower landing, where its crew inspected the hull for damage.

Lock keeper Wilfrid Marchbanks heard a loud splintering noise from the fender and went onto the bridge to inspect the northern approach. He observed a gap of roughly two fingers' width opening between the planking of the northern approach and the main deck, and he closed the southern swing gates by hand. The deck level survey sensors, which record height every two minutes, logged a drop of 4 millimetres in the two hours before impact, within normal seasonal movement. The largest drop in the first hour after impact differs between sources: the survey record gives 31 millimetres, while Marchbanks's notebook gives about 55 millimetres. The survey's final post-impact reading shows the span 31 millimetres below baseline. The Closure Notice identifies the damaged timber fender as the point of impact and states that the bridge will remain shut until a structural engineer has assessed the northern approach span. A bus dispatch record also notes a driver reporting a bump at the northern approach on the run before the closure. The number 14 route has been diverted over the Harcombe road crossing, adding about 9 kilometres to each round trip, and the single-lane bridge with its western footway will remain unavailable until the assessment is complete.

Sources: Skarrowby Canal Trust Closure Notice; Barge master Iolanthe Quillfeather's statement; Skarrowby Tow Bridge Deck Level Survey Record; Lock keeper Wilfrid Marchbanks's notebook; Skarrowby Parish Bus Service Dispatch Record
-----

On a Saturday morning in late September, the Oswin Reach Estuary Trust closed the Oswin Reach Footbridge to all pedestrians and cyclists after pronounced sway developed in the deck during a charity fun run. The estuary was near high water, with a tide gauge reading of 4.1 metres, and the water level was falling slowly by the time the deck was cleared. The timing mat at the western abutment logged 412 runners crossing onto the bridge before the race was halted. Runners were released in a staggered start, and after the first runner stepped onto the western end, runners stopped crossing onto that end.

Race marshal Tamsin Orrelby's notebook records about 260 runners on the deck when the slow-down was first signalled, while Warden Leofric Maddox's statement gives about 340. Both accounts agree that the deck exceeded the posted limit of 300 people at one time. Orrelby observed the handrails visibly swaying from side to side as runners crossed in a dense group, and noted that several runners grabbed the handrails and some stopped near the first tower.

The mid-span deck accelerometer recorded lateral acceleration rising from background levels to 0.34 g within roughly a minute, with a dominant lateral frequency of about 0.9 hertz while the sway was strongest. The sway amplitude decayed after the deck emptied. Maddox walked onto the deck and instructed runners to slow to a walk and spread out. He stated that the deck was cleared on foot toward the eastern bank and that no one was reported injured.

The Closure Log records both gates as locked at 10:22, whereas Maddox's statement gives 10:36 for the same action. This discrepancy should be resolved. The bridge was closed with signs placed at the approach paths, and the Trust has arranged a structural inspection before any reopening can be considered.

Sources: Oswin Reach Estuary Trust Closure Log, Oswin Reach Footbridge Deck Accelerometer Record, Oswin Reach Fun Run Timing Mat Record, Oswin Reach Tide Gauge Record, Race marshal Tamsin Orrelby's notebook, Warden Leofric Maddox's statement
-----

Two pupils at Orrowby Primary School were treated for allergic reactions on 9 September after eating hummus with carrot sticks at lunch. Nurse Imelda Frostwick treated a seven-year-old for hives and lip swelling at 12:40 in the school medical room. A nine-year-old reported throat tightness at 12:55 and was given an adrenaline auto-injector from school stock. Both children were taken by ambulance to Fennick Cross Infirmary and discharged the next morning. Neither child had a peanut allergy recorded in the school health file.

Symptom onset is recorded differently across sources. Dr. Osric Valenmoor's admission notes give 12:10 as the start of the first pupil's symptoms, while Nurse Frostwick recorded onset at 12:25. This discrepancy should be reconciled in the clinical record.

The implicated product was hummus batch HM-0903, blended at the Tarnley District Kitchen from 06:15 on 9 September, portioned into 5-litre tubs, and loaded for delivery at 09:30. The kitchen recipe lists no peanut ingredient. However, the production log shows the blender had been used earlier that week for a satay-style sauce, and the cleaning entry for that blender records a rinse and sanitiser step but no allergen teardown. A retained sample read positive on the allergen test strip reader at 15:20. The reader's calibration check earlier that afternoon was within tolerance. The Halvane Food Analysis Centre later measured peanut protein in the retained sample at 38 milligrams per kilogram and confirmed it in batch HM-0903.

Tubs from the batch were delivered to four schools in the Tarnley district. Kitchen records disagree on how many tubs were held back: the production log lists 14, while supervisor Dorrin Pelch reported 11. This count needs verification.

Sources: Nurse Imelda Frostwick, Dr. Osric Valenmoor, Tarnley District Kitchen production log, Halvane Food Analysis Centre report, Allergen test strip reader, Kitchen supervisor Dorrin Pelch
-----

She reported that several residents developed fever and stomach cramps within two days of the lunch. Inspector Delphine Arkwright of the Vessen County Environmental Health Office collected sealed sample wheels from the cooperative on 22 October following a report of gastrointestinal illness in a Larkmoor client. The inspector ordered the remaining wheels at Larkmoor sealed and labeled as not for use. The cooperative voluntarily paused all sales of raw-milk cheese pending further sampling. On Thursday 23 October, the Vessen Reference Microbiology Unit confirmed Salmonella in wheels from batch HC-1018 using culture-based enrichment followed by serotyping, and identified the isolate as Salmonella Typhimurium.

This incident concerns Salmonella contamination linked to raw-milk soft cheese from batch HC-1018, supplied by the Harrowmere Cheese Cooperative to Larkmoor Residential Catering. The batch was made on 18 October and moved to the aging cellar the following day. Larkmoor received cheese from this batch on 22 October, and the delivery records show a discrepancy in the quantity received: the kitchen manager recorded 60 wheels, while the delivery ledger recorded 48. The cheese was served cold at a Wednesday lunch to residents of two supported-living houses, and several residents later developed fever and stomach cramps within two days of the meal.

Cellar conditions have been examined as a possible contributing factor. The temperature logger recorded a rise from 11.0 degrees Celsius to a peak of 17.4 degrees Celsius during the overnight period of 20 to 21 October, returning below 12 degrees Celsius by mid-morning on 21 October. The cheesemaker reported that the cellar air remained above 12 degrees Celsius for about 9 hours, whereas the logger indicates about 5 hours. This discrepancy has not yet been reconciled. On the morning of 21 October, the cheesemaker also observed the cooling unit's door-panel alarm light lit. The cellar's single compressor serves all three aging rooms, and the logger's internal card should be secured for review.

Environmental Health Inspector Delphine Arkwright collected sealed sample wheels from the cooperative on 22 October and ordered the remaining wheels at Larkmoor sealed and labeled as not for use. The cooperative voluntarily paused all sales of raw-milk cheese pending further sampling. On 23 October, the Vessen Reference Microbiology Unit confirmed Salmonella in wheels from batch HC-1018, identifying the isolate as Salmonella Typhimurium using culture-based enrichment followed by serotyping. Immediate actions for the operations team include reconciling the cellar duration figures, retrieving the logger card, and confirming the status of all remaining wheels.

Sources: Kitchen Manager Odile Penhallow; Harrowmere Cheese Cooperative Cellar Temperature Logger; Vessen Reference Microbiology Unit Report; Inspector Delphine Arkwright of the Vessen County Environmental Health Office; Larkmoor Residential Catering Delivery Ledger; Cheesemaker Tobias Wrenfield
-----

On 9 September, two pupils at Orrowby Primary School developed allergic reactions at lunch after eating hummus with carrot sticks. Nurse Imelda Frostwick treated a seven-year-old for hives and lip swelling at 12:40 in the medical room. A nine-year-old reported throat tightness at 12:55 and was given an adrenaline auto-injector from school stock. Dr. Osric Valenmoor's notes place the first pupil's symptom onset at 12:10, while Nurse Frostwick recorded it at 12:25; this discrepancy should be resolved during the review. Neither child had a peanut allergy recorded in the school health file. Both were transferred by ambulance to Fennick Cross Infirmary and discharged the following morning. Dr. Valenmoor recorded that the two children shared no other food at lunch.

The hummus originated from batch HM-0903, blended at the Tarnley District Kitchen from 06:15 on 9 September, portioned into 5-litre tubs, and loaded for delivery at 09:30. The production log shows the blender had earlier that week been used to prepare a satay-style sauce for a staff event. The cleaning entry for 8 September records a rinse and sanitiser step but no allergen teardown. Kitchen supervisor Dorrin Pelch states the hummus recipe contains no peanut ingredient. A retained sample read positive on the allergen test strip reader at 15:20 that day, and the reader's calibration check earlier that afternoon was within tolerance. The Halvane Food Analysis Centre subsequently measured peanut protein in the retained sample at 38 milligrams per kilogram.

Tubs from the batch were distributed to four schools in the Tarnley district. Following contact from the infirmary, Pelch ordered remaining tubs held in the cold room. The production log lists 14 tubs held back, whereas Pelch reported 11; this count must be reconciled before recall actions are closed. The operations team should confirm cross-contact as the cause, verify the cleaning procedure for shared equipment, and check all distribution points.

Sources: Nurse Imelda Frostwick; Tarnley District Kitchen production log; Dr. Osric Valenmoor; Halvane Food Analysis Centre report; Kitchen supervisor Dorrin Pelch; Allergen test strip reader

Lindenmoor Grange hosted a wedding banquet on Saturday 15 November, and by Monday 17 November the operations team had a laboratory result confirming norovirus in the oysters served on the starter course. This report summarises the facts available as of that date. The Penfarrow Oyster Beds harvest ledger records that lot PO-1112 was harvested on Friday 14 November, a day when the harvest area had been under a heavy-rainfall advisory since 12 November, and that it was dispatched to the venue that afternoon. Accounts of when the oysters left the cooler differ: the banquet manager gives 14:10 on 15 November, the environmental health officer's notes record a cook saying 15:30, and the walk-in cooler logger shows the door open for several minutes at 17:40. Logged air temperatures stayed between 3 and 5 degrees Celsius throughout storage. The oysters were shucked in the kitchen by two cooks that afternoon.

The Skellow Fen Food Safety Laboratory found norovirus genogroup II in four of six sealed oysters tested by RT-PCR. Wennerby Urgent Care has recorded 23 patients with vomiting and diarrhoea who said they attended the wedding, the first registered at 06:15 on 16 November. The environmental health officer found no ill cooks on duty during his inspection on 16 November. Other starter dishes came from separate trays prepared by a different cook. The remaining oysters have been sealed and sent to the laboratory, and guests were notified by message on 17 November.

Sources: Environmental health officer Bram Tolliday's interview notes, Lindenmoor Grange Kitchen Walk-in Cooler Logger, Banquet manager Odile Fanshawe's statement, Penfarrow Oyster Beds Harvest Ledger, Wennerby Urgent Care Clinic Intake Record, Skellow Fen Food Safety Laboratory Report

Incident Report: Undeclared Sesame in Chilled Chicken Noodle Meals, Run CN-0303

This report covers the delivery of chilled chicken noodle meals from production run CN-0303, produced by Thistlewick Meals on Wheels, which were delivered to customer homes on Wednesday 4 March. The Corwen Heath Food Testing Laboratory confirmed undeclared sesame in the meals from this run, finding sesame protein in all three sampled trays from CN-0303 and none in a retained sample from run CN-0302. The trays carried a best-before date of 7 March. The root cause appears to be a labelling error: the printer log shows the allergen template was switched from the sesame-free chicken noodle label to an older generic label at 17:42 on 3 March. That generic label does not list sesame, yet the recipe card for the meal includes a sesame oil dressing sachet. Environmental health officer Gethin Lowrance found that the label template folder had no access control restricting who could change the active template. The printer log lists 212 labels printed under run code CN-0303 between 17:42 and 19:05. The fault was first reported to the kitchen manager at 10:20 on 4 March according to one account and 11:05 according to another, and the discrepancy should be resolved in the final review. Dispatch coordinator Maribel Ashdowne stated that she phoned drivers to halt remaining deliveries after the kitchen manager contacted her, and that a recall notice was issued to all customers on the CN-0303 delivery list the same afternoon. Ms Ashdowne reported that 148 trays had been delivered before deliveries were halted, while the inspection note records 163; this difference also needs reconciling. One customer reported that his seven-year-old daughter, who has a diagnosed sesame allergy, developed hives and a swollen lip after eating part of a meal at lunch. Her symptoms eased after antihistamine and no hospital visit was required. The cold van recorder for van 3 shows interior temperatures between 2.1 and 4.4 degrees Celsius throughout the round, so temperature control does not appear to be a contributing factor.

The Listeria monocytogenes incident involving vacuum-packed smoked trout from Quenby Smokehouse was identified when the Brindlemoor Public Health Laboratory confirmed the organism on Saturday 14 June in a sample taken from an unopened 250-gram pack of lot code QT-0611, sold at Wickerby Lakeside Market that morning. The laboratory report records a detected level above 100 colony-forming units per gram, following 48 hours of enrichment and growth on selective agar. The production log shows that lot QT-0611 was smoked and packed on Wednesday 11 June and contains 184 packs.

Sales figures for the market stall remain inconsistent. The vendor, Marisol Quenby, reported 42 packs from the lot sold on 14 June, while the market manager, Tobias Ferrant, reported 67. This gap must be resolved before the recall scope is finalised. Mr. Ferrant estimated that about 60 shoppers stopped at the stall during the morning.

Cold-chain records show the smokehouse cold room held a steady 3.5 degrees Celsius for most of the week, with a spike to 9.2 degrees Celsius on the night of Thursday 12 June. At the market, packs are displayed on crushed ice in insulated boxes, but the market does not provide refrigeration for vendor stalls, which sit under open-sided canopies near the lake shore. Exposure conditions at the stall remain an open line of inquiry.

Dr. Halvard Teague, the county environmental health officer, visited the smokehouse on Saturday afternoon, ordered swabs of the slicing table, brine tanks, and processing room drain, and issued a stop-sale order covering all smoked fish products. Dr. Teague recorded that the order reached the stall at about 1:10 p.m., while Mr. Ferrant recorded about 1:45 p.m.; this discrepancy should be reconciled against call logs. Mr. Ferrant stopped trout sales within minutes of receiving the call. Ms. Quenby notified regular customers by phone and posted a notice on the smokehouse door that evening. The production log records that brine tanks are emptied and sanitised on Mondays, a schedule to be checked against the sampling results.

Sources: Marisol Quenby, owner of Quenby Smokehouse; Quenby Smokehouse production log; Tobias Ferrant, market manager at Wickerby Lakeside Market; Dr. Halvard Teague, county environmental health officer; Brindlemoor Public Health Laboratory report; Cold-room temperature data logger at Quenby Smokehouse

Incident Report: Undeclared Sesame in Chilled Chicken Noodle Meals, Run CN-0303

Environmental health officer Gethin Lowrance found that the label template folder had no access control restricting who could change the active template. The printer log records 212 labels printed under run code CN-0303 between 17:42 and 19:05.

Dispatch coordinator Maribel Ashdowne stated that she phoned drivers to halt remaining deliveries after the kitchen manager contacted her, and that a recall notice was issued to all customers on the CN-0303 delivery list the same afternoon. The number of trays delivered before the halt is also disputed: Ms Ashdowne stated 148, while the inspection note records 163. A customer reported that his seven-year-old daughter, who has a diagnosed sesame allergy, developed hives and a swollen lip after eating part of a meal at lunch. Her symptoms eased after antihistamine, and no hospital visit was required. The cold van recorder for van 3 shows interior temperatures between 2.1 and 4.4 degrees Celsius throughout the round, so temperature control does not appear to be a contributing factor.

The Corwen Heath Food Testing Laboratory confirmed sesame protein in all three sampled trays from run CN-0303, and none in a retained sample from the earlier run CN-0302. The affected trays carried a best-before date of 7 March.

The most likely root cause is a label template fault. The printer log shows that the allergen template was switched from the sesame-free chicken noodle label to an older generic label at 17:42 on 3 March. Environmental health officer Gethin Lowrance also found that the label template folder had no access control restricting who could change the active template, which allowed the change to occur without a controlled check.

The timing of the first report needs reconciling. Dispatch records show the fault was first reported to the kitchen manager at 10:20 on 4 March, while a customer account gives 11:05. Vans were loaded at 06:30 and began drops at 07:15. Dispatch later halted remaining deliveries, but the number of trays delivered before the halt differs between two accounts, 148 and 163. This discrepancy must be resolved. A recall notice was issued to all customers on the delivery list the same afternoon.

One customer reported that his seven-year-old daughter, who has a diagnosed sesame allergy, developed hives and a swollen lip after lunch. Her symptoms eased with antihistamine and no hospital visit was required. Cold chain records for van 3 show interior temperatures between 2.1 and 4.4 degrees Celsius throughout the round, so temperature control does not appear to be a contributing factor.
