On 9 October at 18:42, the dialysis and imaging wing of Veyra Lowlands Medical Centre lost mains power following a fault trip recorded on the 11 kV feeder serving the site. The wing transferred to its battery-backed supply, and the UPS controller record indicates the load was taken over with no gap in output voltage. At changeover the battery bank was supplying 38 kilowatts, and a low-battery pre-alarm was logged on the UPS bank at 19:31. Six dialysis machines were running patient sessions at the time of changeover. The charge nurse reports that all sessions were completed without any machine being stopped. Two patients reported feeling cold when the dialysis room ventilation fans paused. Security confirmed that emergency lighting was operating and that the main doors functioned normally. The MRI scanner was in standby with no scan in progress. The facilities engineer recorded the battery cabinet temperature at 24 degrees Celsius and noted the bank is rated for roughly 90 minutes at the load being drawn. The rest of the medical centre remained on mains throughout the event.

The sources disagree on two points that must be reconciled before this report is finalised. The grid operator's report attributes the feeder trip solely to a cable joint failure at the Orrin Mews substation and gives a battery run time of 64 minutes. The facilities engineer attributes the trip to a protection relay fault at the site's own incoming switchgear, while the UPS record shows mains returning after 51 minutes. The fault cause and the recorded run time should be confirmed against primary data.

Incident Report: Power Loss to Dialysis and Imaging Wing, Veyra Lowlands Medical Centre

The supply has since been restored to mains and the battery bank is recharging. The rest of the medical centre remained on mains throughout the event. Security confirmed that emergency lighting was active, that main doors were operating normally, and that the MRI scanner was in standby with no scan in progress. Security also escorted electricians to the switchroom. The facilities engineer recorded the battery cabinet temperature at 24 degrees Celsius and noted that the battery bank is rated for roughly 90 minutes at the load drawn. The sources disagree on the cause of the feeder trip. The grid operator attributes it to a cable joint failure at the Orrin Mews substation, while the facilities engineer attributes it to a protection relay fault in the medical centre's own incoming switchgear. The differing outage durations and the conflicting cause attributions should be reconciled before the cause is recorded as final.

Sources: Switchboard UPS Controller Record, Veyra Lowlands Medical Centre Building Management System Event Log, Nurse Imogen Tavish, Wennock Grid Services Fault Report, Security officer Halla Brindt, Facilities engineer Dorian Peaswick

Sources: Nurse Imelda Frostwick, Dr. Osric Valenmoor, Tarnley District Kitchen production log, Halvane Food Analysis Centre report, Kitchen supervisor Dorrin Pelch, Allergen test strip reader

Thistlewick Meals on Wheels produced chilled chicken noodle meals under production run CN-0303. On 4 March, the Corwen Heath Food Testing Laboratory confirmed undeclared sesame in trays from that run. The laboratory report records sesame protein in all three sampled trays from CN-0303 and none in a retained sample from run CN-0302, and it states that the tested trays carried a best-before date of 7 March. The printer log shows that the allergen template was switched from the sesame-free chicken noodle label to the older generic label at 17:42 on 3 March, and 212 labels were printed under run code CN-0303 between 17:42 and 19:05. The generic label on those trays does not list sesame, although the recipe card for the meal includes a sesame oil dressing sachet. Environmental health inspection found that the label template folder had no access control restricting who could change the active template.

The label template fault was first reported to the kitchen manager. The sources give differing times of 10:20 and 11:05 on 4 March, and the review should reconcile these. Vans were loaded at 06:30 and began the first drops at 07:15 that morning. The sources differ on the number of affected trays delivered before halting, with dispatch recording 148 and inspection recording 163. Dispatch states that drivers were phoned to halt remaining deliveries after the kitchen manager raised the label fault, and that a recall notice was sent to all customers on the CN-0303 delivery list the same afternoon. The cold van recorder for van 3 shows an interior temperature between 2.1 and 4.4 degrees Celsius throughout its round, and the rear door opened 31 times during the morning round.

One customer reported that his seven-year-old daughter, who has a diagnosed sesame allergy, developed hives and a swollen lip after eating part of a meal at lunch. He stated that he checked the label before serving, that antihistamine eased her symptoms, and that no hospital visit was needed.

Sources: Corwen Heath Food Testing Laboratory Report, Dispatch coordinator Maribel Ashdowne's statement, Customer Ewan Parkhallow's account, Thistlewick Meals on Wheels Production Label Printer Log, Thistlewick Meals on Wheels Cold Van Temperature Recorder Printout, Environmental health officer Gethin Lowrance's inspection note

The power loss affecting Ward 4, the cardiac step-down unit at St. Brannock Infirmary, began at 02:17 on 14 March. Mains supply to the hospital was lost following a fault on an 11 kV feeder north of the building, which tripped supply to roughly 3,200 customers. The hospital's diesel backup generators started, and Generator A reached rated speed and accepted load at 02:17 and 41 seconds. The generator controller recorded the hospital returning to mains supply at 04:10 after a retransfer sequence. The utility bulletin states that supply to the hospital's street was restored at 03:52. Ward 4 held 14 patients in its 18 beds that night.

According to charge nurse Imelda Torrance, the ward's general lighting and white outlets were without power for about 25 minutes. The facilities log gives a figure of about 48 minutes, and this discrepancy must be resolved by the review. Torrance reported that the red-outlet sockets remained live, that two patients on portable infusion pumps were moved to bedside positions beside red sockets, and that the Ward 4 telemetry monitors continued displaying heart rhythms on their internal batteries.

On-call facilities engineer Davor Quillfeather found the main breaker for the Ward 4 lighting and general-outlet panel open and attended the plant room to inspect the transfer switchgear. The facilities log records that the panel breaker was closed by hand, after which the ward's general outlets were live again. The sources give conflicting accounts of why the breaker was open. One attributes it to a trip on an overload surge when the generator took the load; another attributes it to the breaker having been left open by earlier maintenance work and never reclosed. The controller logged 410 kW on Generator A shortly after reconnection. The day tank stood at 82 percent when the outage began, and the planned monthly generator test was last completed on 2 March.

This review should establish the cause of the open breaker, reconcile the outage duration, and assess whether the generator test schedule was adequate.

Sources: Nurse Imelda Torrance (charge nurse, Ward 4); Northmere Electric Distribution outage bulletin; Engineer Davor Quillfeather (on-call facilities engineer); Generator controller event record; Facilities log of St. Brannock Infirmary

**Incident Report: Salmonella Contamination Linked to Raw-Milk Soft Cheese, Batch HC-1018**

This report sets out the facts established so far concerning Salmonella contamination associated with raw-milk soft cheese from batch HC-1018, supplied by the Harrowmere Cheese Cooperative to Larkmoor Residential Catering. The batch was made on 18 October and moved to the aging cellar the following day. Larkmoor received cheese from this batch on 22 October. The kitchen manager recorded 60 wheels, each weighing about 400 grams, while the delivery ledger records 48 wheels, a difference that must be resolved. The cheese was served cold at a Wednesday lunch to residents of two supported-living houses, and several residents later developed fever and stomach cramps within two days of the meal.

Cellar conditions were examined as a possible contributing factor. The temperature logger recorded a rise from 11.0 degrees Celsius to a peak of 17.4 degrees Celsius during the overnight period of 20 to 21 October, with readings returning below 12 degrees Celsius by mid-morning on 21 October. The cheesemaker reported that the cellar air stayed above 12 degrees Celsius for about 9 hours, while the logger indicates about 5 hours, and this discrepancy remains unreconciled. The cheesemaker also found the cooling unit's door-panel alarm light lit on the morning of 21 October. A single compressor unit serves all three aging rooms. The logger stores its readings on an internal card, which should be secured for review.

Environmental Health Inspector Delphine Arkwright collected sealed sample wheels from the cooperative on 22 October and ordered the remaining wheels at Larkmoor sealed and labeled as not for use. The cooperative voluntarily paused all sales of raw-milk cheese pending further sampling. On 23 October, the Vessen Reference Microbiology Unit confirmed Salmonella in wheels from batch HC-1018, identified as Salmonella Typhimurium using culture-based enrichment followed by serotyping. Immediate actions for the operations team include reconciling the cellar duration figures and the wheel counts, retrieving the logger card, and confirming the status of all remaining wheels.

Sources: Kitchen Manager Odile Penhallow; Harrowmere Cheese Cooperative Cellar Temperature Logger; Vessen Reference Microbiology Unit Report; Inspector Delphine Arkwright of the Vessen County Environmental Health Office; Larkmoor Residential Catering Delivery Ledger; Cheesemaker Tobias Wrenfield

St. Brannock Infirmary experienced a power interruption beginning at 02:17 on 14 March, when mains supply was lost and the building transferred to its diesel backup generators. The generator controller recorded that mains voltage fell below its threshold at that time and issued start commands to Generator A and Generator B. Generator A reached rated speed and accepted load at 02:17 and 41 seconds. The hospital returned to mains supply at 04:10 following a retransfer sequence. According to the external utility's outage bulletin, the cause was a fault on an 11 kV feeder north of the hospital that tripped supply to roughly 3,200 customers. The feeder was re-energized by switching to an alternate route, and supply to the hospital's street was restored at 03:52.

Ward 4, an 18-bed cardiac step-down unit, held 14 patients that night. The charge nurse reported that general lighting and white outlets were without power for about 25 minutes, while red-outlet sockets remained live and telemetry monitors continued operating on internal batteries. Two patients on portable infusion pumps were moved to bedside positions beside red sockets. The facilities log records the white-outlet and lighting interruption as about 48 minutes, a discrepancy with the nurse's estimate that the review should reconcile.

The on-call facilities engineer found the main breaker for the Ward 4 lighting and general-outlet panel in the open position and closed it by hand, restoring power to the ward's general outlets. The facilities log states the breaker had been left open by earlier maintenance and never reclosed. The engineer's account instead attributes the open position solely to a trip on an overload surge when the generator took the load. The generator controller logged 410 kW on Generator A shortly after the panel was reconnected. These accounts conflict, and the review should establish which explanation the evidence supports. The facilities log also notes the generator day tank was at 82 percent when the outage began and that the planned monthly generator test was last completed on 2 March.

Sources: Nurse Imelda Torrance (charge nurse, Ward 4), Northmere Electric Distribution outage bulletin, Engineer Davor Quillfeather (on-call facilities engineer), Generator controller event record, Facilities log of St. Brannock Infirmary

Mr Tolliday's inspection on 16 November found no cooks on duty reporting illness, and the other starter dishes were served from separate trays prepared by a different cook.

Wennerby Urgent Care Clinic has recorded 23 patients presenting with vomiting and diarrhoea between 16 and 17 November who reported attending the wedding, the first registered at 06:15 on 16 November. Incident Report: Undeclared Sesame in Chicken Noodle Meals, Production Run CN-0303

This report covers chilled chicken noodle meals from production run CN-0303, prepared by Thistlewick Meals on Wheels and delivered on Wednesday 4 March with a best-before date of 7 March. The Corwen Heath Food Testing Laboratory confirmed undeclared sesame protein in all three sampled trays from run CN-0303, while a retained sample from run CN-0302 contained none. The generic label template printed on these trays does not list sesame, although the recipe card includes a sesame oil dressing sachet. The omission from the label is the apparent root cause.

The printer log shows that the allergen template was switched from the sesame-free chicken noodle label to the older generic label at 17:42 on 3 March, and that 212 labels were printed under run code CN-0303 between 17:42 and 19:05. The environmental health officer found that the kitchen's label template folder had no access control restricting who could change the active template, so the change could be made without oversight. Vans were loaded at 06:30 on 4 March and began the first drops at 07:15. The fault was reported to the kitchen manager at 10:20 according to dispatch records and at 11:05 according to a customer account; this discrepancy is still to be resolved. Drivers were phoned to halt remaining deliveries once the fault was raised, and a recall notice was issued to all customers on the delivery list the same afternoon.

Dispatch records differ on how many trays reached homes before deliveries were halted: the dispatch coordinator's statement gives 148, while the inspection note gives 163. One customer reported that his seven-year-old daughter, who has a diagnosed sesame allergy, developed hives and a swollen lip after eating part of the meal at lunch. Her symptoms eased with antihistamine and no hospital visit was required. The cold van recorder for van 3 showed interior temperatures between 2.1 and 4.4 degrees Celsius throughout its round, indicating that cold chain control was not a contributing factor.

Production run CN-0303 of chilled chicken noodle meals, manufactured by Thistlewick Meals on Wheels and delivered on Wednesday 4 March, was found by the Corwen Heath Food Testing Laboratory to contain undeclared sesame. Sesame protein was detected in all three sampled trays from this run, while a retained sample from the earlier run CN-0302 showed none. The affected trays carried a best-before date of 7 March. The probable root cause is a label template fault. The printer log shows that the allergen template was switched from the sesame-free chicken noodle label to an older generic label at 17:42 on 3 March, and 212 labels were printed under run code CN-0303 between 17:42 and 19:05. The generic label does not list sesame, although the recipe card includes a sesame oil dressing sachet. Environmental health officer Gethin Lowrance also found that the label template folder had no access control restricting who could change the active template.

The fault was first reported to the kitchen manager at 10:20 on 4 March according to dispatch records, but at 11:05 according to a customer account. This discrepancy needs to be reconciled. Vans were loaded at 06:30 and began drops at 07:15. Dispatch later halted remaining deliveries. The number of trays delivered before the halt is recorded as 148 in one account and 163 in another, which also requires resolution. A recall notice was issued to all customers on the delivery list the same afternoon. One customer reported that his seven-year-old daughter, who has a diagnosed sesame allergy, developed hives and a swollen lip after lunch. Her symptoms eased with antihistamine and no hospital visit was required. Cold chain records for van 3 show interior temperatures between 2.1 and 4.4 degrees Celsius throughout the round, so temperature control does not appear to be a contributing factor.

Eight volunteers from Ravensholt Mountain Rescue reached the site on foot from the road, and floodlights were set up along the embankment shortly after their arrival. The timing of the evacuation differs between records: the conductor's record gives 20:40 as the time the last passenger was led off the train, while the rescue record gives 20:05 and notes that the evacuation took place after dark. This discrepancy should be reconciled before the timeline is finalised.

The Ravensholt Embankment Tilt Sensor recorded a sudden change of 2.4 degrees in slope angle beside the track and continued to log readings throughout the evening, indicating slow further movement of the slope. A team of eight volunteers from Ravensholt Mountain Rescue reached the site on foot from the road, and floodlights were set up along the embankment shortly after their arrival. The incident involved the 18:12 diesel service from Ravensholt to Garrowmere, a four-carriage unit carrying passengers from Ravensholt Central. Rain had been falling steadily across the Tolvane valley since early afternoon. At approximately 18:31 on a Friday in late October, the two rear carriages derailed on the Tolvane Viaduct approach. Prior to the derailment, the train was travelling at about 35 km/h when the driver applied the emergency brake. The signaller lost track-circuit indication for the Tolvane section at the moment the train stopped, and Control logged the Garrowmere-bound line as blocked to all traffic from that point. The signaller also held the following freight service at Ravensholt Yard after the alarm.

Passenger numbers on board remain disputed. The stationmaster recorded 58 passengers, while the conductor recorded 46. Conductor Oyelaran walked through the train, reported that lights remained on in the front two carriages, and instructed passengers to stay seated until rescuers confirmed the ground beside the train was safe. Eight volunteers from Ravensholt Mountain Rescue reached the site on foot from the road, and floodlights were set up along the embankment shortly after their arrival. The records differ on evacuation timing: the conductor's record gives 20:40 as the time the last passenger was led off the train, while the rescue record gives 20:05 and notes that evacuation took place after dark. This discrepancy should be reconciled in the final review.

The Ravensholt Embankment Tilt Sensor recorded a sudden change of 2.4 degrees in the slope angle beside the track and continued to transmit readings throughout the evening, indicating slow further movement of the slope. Stationmaster Drevenak arranged coaches to convey passengers onward to Garrowmere once they had been brought to the road, and cancelled the remaining evening departures from Ravensholt Central.

Sources: Conductor Maribel Oyelaran, Ravensholt Rail Control Log, Signaller Idris Vantongeren, Ravensholt Mountain Rescue Incident Record, Ravensholt Embankment Tilt Sensor, Stationmaster Hollis Drevenak

No baby was transferred to another hospital because of the outage.

The switchboard log gives about 3 hours 40 minutes on generator power before mains returned, while the generator log records about 4 hours 25 minutes. This discrepancy should be checked. The derailment of ore train 3306 from Veshurst Mine occurred on the Dunstable Cutting reverse curve of the Pemberly Ore Line shortly after 02:10 on a Sunday in mid-January. The incident involved the 18:12 service from Ravensholt to Garrowmere, a four-carriage diesel unit carrying passengers from Ravensholt Central. The train was running at about 35 km/h when the driver applied the emergency brake. The Ravensholt Rail Control Log records that the last two carriages derailed on the Tolvane Viaduct approach at about 18:31 on a Friday in late October, during a period of steady rain across the Tolvane valley since early afternoon. Following the stop, Signaller Vantongeren lost the track-circuit indication for the Tolvane section, held the following freight service at Ravensholt Yard, and control logged the Garrowmere-bound line as blocked to all traffic.

Passenger numbers differ between two accounts. Stationmaster Drevenak recorded 58 passengers aboard at the time of derailment, while Conductor Oyelaran recorded 46. The conductor walked through the train, reported that lighting remained on in the front two carriages, and instructed passengers to remain seated until rescuers confirmed the ground beside the train was safe. Eight volunteers from Ravensholt Mountain Rescue reached the site on foot from the road and set up floodlights along the embankment shortly after arrival. The Ravensholt Mountain Rescue Incident Record gives 20:05 as the time the last passenger was led off the train, whereas Conductor Oyelaran gives 20:40. This discrepancy must be reconciled before the timeline is finalised.

The embankment tilt sensor recorded a sudden 2.4-degree change in slope angle beside the track and continued to show slow further movement through the evening, indicating ground instability that should be assessed before any line reopening. Stationmaster Drevenak arranged coaches to carry passengers onward to Garrowmere and cancelled the remaining evening departures from Ravensholt Central.

Sources: Conductor Maribel Oyelaran, Ravensholt Rail Control Log, Signaller Idris Vantongeren, Ravensholt Mountain Rescue Incident Record, Ravensholt Embankment Tilt Sensor, Stationmaster Hollis Drevenak

The gates remained open until the release ended, and the sensor recorded both gates beginning to close at 6:05 p.m.

Marisol Quade, who operates a canoe rental business beside Pellam Ford, had aluminum canoes stacked on a gravel bar roughly forty meters from the normal waterline. Quade observed water covering the bar and lifting the lowest canoes, and moved several canoes to higher ground before the water reached the rental shed. Marisol Quade, who operates a canoe rental business beside Pellam Ford, had aluminum canoes stacked on a gravel bar roughly forty meters from the normal waterline. Quade observed water covering the bar and lifting the lowest canoes, and moved several canoes to higher ground before the water reached the rental shed. Quade reported that eleven canoes were swept downstream from the bar, while Vance's account refers to seven. The review should reconcile this difference in the canoe count.

Her patrol report describes brown water carrying branches and reeds, a wooden fishing platform on the left bank lifted from its posts and carried downstream, and fourteen rods lost from the landing rack. The angling club secretary, Wilmot Dree, reported that rod racks had been stacked on clubhouse tables after the notice, recorded nine rods lost from the landing rack, and stated that the club's rowing skiff broke its mooring line and drifted away. The derailment of ore train 3306 from Veshurst Mine took place on the Dunstable Cutting reverse curve of the Pemberly Ore Line shortly after 02:10 on a Sunday in mid-January. The train consisted of one locomotive and 22 loaded ore wagons, with a recorded gross load of 1,640 tonnes of iron ore. The driver, Teodora Brannigan, was the only crew member in the cab and was not injured. She reported dry conditions with patchy fog and described a sideways jolt through the cab floor before applying the emergency brake. The signalling log places the brake application at 02:15, while her own statement gives 02:13, and this discrepancy should be reconciled during review.

Three wagons from the middle of the train left the rails, and two of them tipped onto their sides across the adjacent line, spilling ore over roughly 40 metres of track. The locomotive and the first 11 wagons remained on the rails and stopped beyond the curve. The signalling log shows the train passing the entry signal at 38 kilometres per hour against a line speed limit of 40 kilometres per hour. The track circuit through the curve failed to clear after the train passed.

The inspector found water standing against the outer rail before the train arrived. The pump house recorder shows one of two pumps stopped from 01:20 onward, with the drainage sump reaching 2.9 metres at midnight, about 0.6 metres above its alarm threshold. A track geometry survey from the previous week had already recorded gauge widening of 9 millimetres beyond tolerance on the curve. Locomotive wheel profiles were within limits when measured the following day, which points away from the rolling stock as a primary contributor.

Further review should focus on drainage performance, including the pump failure and the response to the high sump level, the condition of the curve in light of the gauge widening, and the reliability of the track circuit, which did not clear after the train passed.

The 06:48 railcar service from Sedgley Halt to Marrowby Cross, a two-car diesel unit on the single-track Tamlin Fen Light Railway, derailed its front axle on the Tamlin Fen embankment at approximately 07:02 on a Thursday in late November. The washout sensor beside the embankment first registered ballast displacement at 06:52 according to the maintenance register, but the sensor's own record gives 06:57. The washout left a gap in the ballast roughly 12 metres long beneath the down rail. The maintenance register notes that the embankment had last been inspected on foot nine days before the derailment.

The driver reported a sudden lurch, applied the brakes, and brought the railcar to a stop within about 90 metres. He then shut down the engines and secured the railcar with the handbrake. The railcar came to rest tilted about 15 degrees toward the drainage ditch. Passenger counts differ between accounts: the driver's statement records twenty-seven passengers aboard, while the conductor's report records twenty-three. Immediately after the stop, the conductor walked the length of both cars, reported four passengers with bruises or minor cuts from being thrown against seat frames, and kept passengers inside the cars until the driver confirmed the line was blocked in both directions. The signaller stopped all traffic and placed the section under block at 07:05. A road coach has been arranged to carry passengers on to Marrowby Cross once they have left the railcar. The passenger discrepancy and the sensor timing discrepancy should both be addressed in the final review findings.

The derailment of ore train 3306 from Veshurst Mine occurred on the Dunstable Cutting reverse curve of the Pemberly Ore Line shortly after 02:10 on a Sunday in mid-January. The train comprised one locomotive and 22 loaded ore wagons carrying a recorded gross load of 1,640 tonnes of iron ore. The driver, Teodora Brannigan, was the sole crew member in the cab and sustained no injuries. She reported dry conditions with patchy fog and described a sideways jolt through the cab floor before applying the emergency brake. The signalling log records the brake application at 02:15, whereas her own statement gives 02:13. This discrepancy should be reconciled during review.

Three wagons from the middle of the train left the rails, and two of them tipped onto their sides across the adjacent line, spilling ore over roughly 40 metres of track. The locomotive and the first 11 wagons remained on the rails and stopped beyond the curve. The signalling log shows the train passing the entry signal at 38 kilometres per hour against a line speed limit of 40 kilometres per hour. The track circuit through the curve failed to clear after the train passed.

The inspector found water standing against the outer rail before the train arrived. The pump house recorder shows that one of two pumps had stopped from 01:20 onward, and the drainage sump reached 2.9 metres at midnight, about 0.6 metres above its alarm threshold. A track geometry survey from the previous week had already recorded gauge widening of 9 millimetres beyond tolerance on the curve. Locomotive wheel profiles measured the following day were within limits, which points away from the rolling stock as a primary contributor.

Further review should focus on drainage performance, including the pump failure and the response to the high sump level, the condition of the curve in light of the gauge widening, and the reliability of the track circuit, which did not clear after the train passed.

The Stillwater Narrows Dam opened its number 1 sluice spillway gate at 9:50 a.m. on 17 February to release water from Perrin Mere into the Cobbet River. The station also logged a sharp rise in turbidity soon after the water arrived and a drop in river temperature of about 2 degrees Celsius as colder lake water came through. Allotment warden Edda Marnock observed river water spilling over the lowest allotment path and into the plots nearest the bank, and advised plot holders to move tools and compost bins away from the riverbank. Accounts of the number of wheelbarrows carried off the lowest path differ, with the patrol notebook recording eleven and Marnock's account recording seven. Incident Report: Controlled Release from Lake Oswin, Marrick Sill Dam, 22 September

On 22 September, the Marrick Sill Dam Authority initiated a controlled release from Lake Oswin at 4:35 p.m. to lower the lake before it reached its upper operating limit. According to the release notice, the drum gate was to be fully closed once the lake had dropped by 1.2 metres. The lake gauge recorded 211.4 metres just before the gate began to move, fell steadily over the first hour, and settled at 210.2 metres after closure.

The dam operator, Teodor Hallam, recorded sounding the warning horn for thirty seconds before the first stage. The gate was raised in three stages with a ten-minute pause after each and lowered to the closed position once the target level was reached. The Harrap Beck flow meter rose from 3 to 46 cubic metres per second over the first ninety minutes, with a brief dip at 5:50 p.m. before the rise resumed. The peak flow at the hamlet is recorded as 6:25 p.m. in the flow meter record but 6:55 p.m. in the operator's notebook. This discrepancy requires reconciliation.

On the ground, Ranger Ines Carrowby closed the gravel path to the hamlet with two red barriers and reported brown water carrying branches and reeds past the hamlet. She also reported that a wooden fishing platform on the left bank was lifted from its posts and floated downstream, and that fourteen rods were lost from the landing rack. The angling club secretary, Wilmot Dree, stated that the club had stacked its rod racks on clubhouse tables after receiving the notice, that nine rods were lost from the landing rack, and that the club's rowing skiff snapped its mooring line and drifted away. The rod loss figures differ between the two accounts and must be verified. Operations should review the timing discrepancy, the rod count, and the status of the skiff and platform.

Sources: Oswin Lake Level Gauge Record; Dam operator Teodor Hallam's shift notebook; Harrap Beck Flow Meter Record; Harrap Beck Angling Club secretary Wilmot Dree's account; Ranger Ines Carrowby's patrol report; Marrick Sill Dam Authority Release Notice

Okafor-Lund asked the terminal duty manager to pause new check-in bag acceptance for a short period.

She reports that the flock had been brought down from winter shelter that week. She heard the siren from the pasture gate and began driving the animals toward higher ground. Spillway water reached the lower pasture and covered the Quillon Brook track. Accounts differ on how long the flooding lasted, with Haskett describing about four hours and the operator describing about two hours. Livestock losses are also reported differently. Haskett reports seven sheep swept off their feet, while the Vesper Hollow Grazing Association Notice reports eleven. That notice had directed members to keep stock off the Quillon Brook pasture until further advice and named the Alder Lane stock gate as the assembly point for animals moved off the pasture.

Sources: Imogen Haskett, shepherd; Tolliver Weir Dam Operations Log; Marten Oyelaran, dam operator on shift; Vesper Hollow Grazing Association Notice; Greenhallow Reservoir Level Recorder

Warden Teodor Marsk moved picnic tables in the lower tent area to higher ground and personally woke the occupants of the eleven tents pitched that morning. The Stillwater Narrows Dam opened its number 1 sluice spillway gate at 9:50 a.m. on 17 February to release water from Perrin Mere into the Cobbet River. The release was ordered to lower the lake ahead of a scheduled inspection of the intake tower, and the release notice stated that the gate would remain open until the lake had fallen by 0.6 metres. Gate operator Hallam Rooke raised the gate in two stages, first to a quarter opening and then to a half opening, and recorded a loud, steady roar from the stilling basin once it reached half opening. A warning notice was posted at the Ostlewick footpath stile roughly 40 minutes before the gate opened. Volunteers with the Ostlewick Footpath Volunteer Patrol closed the lower footpath with tape at both ends of the riverside section, and two walkers turned back at the tape and used the road instead.

At the sonde station, 3.2 kilometres below the dam beside the Ostlewick footbridge, the station record shows the river peaking at 1.8 metres above its normal level. Hallam Rooke's statement gives a higher peak of 2.3 metres for the same station, and this discrepancy must be reconciled during the review. The station also logged a sharp rise in turbidity soon after the water arrived and a drop in river temperature of about 2 degrees Celsius as colder lake water came through. Allotment warden Edda Marnock observed river water spilling over the lowest allotment path and into the plots nearest the bank, and advised plot holders to move tools and compost bins away from the riverbank. Accounts of the number of wheelbarrows carried off the lowest path differ, with the patrol notebook recording eleven and Marnock's account recording seven. The inflow gauge shows Perrin Mere inflow steady at about 6 cubic metres per second throughout the morning. The gate was lowered to closed the same afternoon once the target lake level was reached.

Haskett reports that seven sheep were swept off their feet, while the Vesper Hollow Grazing Association Notice gives a figure of eleven. This discrepancy remains unresolved.

The track along Quillon Brook stayed under water for a period that sources describe differently: about four hours according to Haskett and about two hours according to Oyelaran. At 06:42 on a Tuesday, the main outbound sortation line at Corvane Island Airport stopped after the Sorter Control System Event Record logged an emergency stop on the main sortation loop at 06:42:17. Drive motor current on the loop dropped to zero at the moment of the stop. The loop was restarted at 13:05, and automated sorting did not resume until early afternoon. Three Skerrin Air departures scheduled between 07:15 and 09:00 were affected. The first of these departed with a delay measured in minutes rather than hours, as bags were matched to passengers before it was released. The last affected departure left only after the loop was restored.

The cause of the emergency stop has not been established because the accounts of those involved conflict. Ines Okafor-Lund, the baggage hall shift supervisor, who was directing a crew of nine at the time, attributed the stop solely to an oversized bag striking the loop's guard rail and tripping the safety circuit. Halvard Quist, the maintenance technician, who reached the sorter hall within about fifteen minutes of being called, reported finding a diverter arm jammed near the third merge point and stated that this arm alone caused the stop. He also noted that the pneumatic fitting on the diverter arm was warm to the touch. Because these two explanations are mutually exclusive as stated, the cause should be confirmed against the physical evidence, including the guard rail, the diverter arm, and the safety circuit data.

The operational response included a request from Okafor-Lund to the terminal duty manager to pause new check-in bag acceptance for a short period. Handlers hand-carried bags from the check-in belts to aircraft carts, and the Operations Log records that two additional handlers were brought in from the cargo shed. The number of hand-carried bags also differs between sources. The Operations Log cites 164, while ground handling agent Tamsin Reyes cites 212. Reyes further recalled the hand-carrying area filling with suitcases stacked two or three high along the wall, which suggests the backlog may have exceeded what the Operations Log records.

Sources: Halvard Quist, Ines Okafor-Lund, Tamsin Reyes, Sorter Control System Event Record, Corvane Island Airport Operations Log, Skerrin Air Departure Control Record

Downstream effects were significant. The river at the sonde station 3.2 kilometres below the dam, beside the Ostlewick footbridge, peaked at a level that the records describe differently: 1.8 metres above normal in the sonde station record and 2.3 metres in the gate operator's statement. The Marrick Sill Dam Authority opened the drum gate at Lake Oswin at 4:35 p.m. on 22 September to begin a staged spillway release intended to lower the lake before it reached its upper operating limit. Under the release notice, the gate was to be fully closed once the lake had dropped by 1.2 metres. The lake stood at 211.4 metres before the gate moved, fell steadily during the first hour, and settled at 210.2 metres after closure.

Dam operator Teodor Hallam's shift notebook records a thirty-second warning horn before the first stage, three gate-raising stages with a ten-minute pause after each, and closure once the target level was reached. The Harrap Beck flow meter shows discharge rising from 3 to 46 cubic metres per second over the first ninety minutes, with a brief dip at 5:50 p.m. before the rise resumed. The meter logged peak flow at the hamlet at 6:25 p.m., whereas Hallam's notebook gives the peak as 6:55 p.m. This discrepancy must be reconciled against clock settings before the timeline is finalised.

Downstream impacts were recorded by Ranger Ines Carrowby, who closed the gravel path to the hamlet with two red barriers and reported brown water carrying branches and reeds past the hamlet. A wooden fishing platform on the left bank was lifted from its posts and carried downstream. Angling club secretary Wilmot Dree reported that the club had stacked its rod racks on clubhouse tables after receiving the notice, that nine rods were lost from the landing rack during the surge, and that the club's rowing skiff snapped its mooring line and drifted away. Carrowby's account gives a loss of fourteen rods from the same rack. The two figures differ and require verification before any loss estimate is recorded.

Sources: Oswin Lake Level Gauge Record, Dam operator Teodor Hallam's shift notebook, Harrap Beck Flow Meter Record, Harrap Beck Angling Club secretary Wilmot Dree's account, Ranger Ines Carrowby's patrol report, Marrick Sill Dam Authority Release Notice

The oversize baggage belt at Skellmark Harbour Airport stopped at 14:08 on a Wednesday after the belt controller logged an overload trip on the transfer conveyor drive, and it did not return to automatic mode until 17:44. The photo-eye counter recorded no items entering the belt during the outage and registered 61 items passing in the two hours before the stop. A maintenance technician opened the transfer conveyor guard at 14:31 and found the drive coupling hot to the touch. The maintenance work order records that a replacement drive coupling was fitted and the overload relay reset before the belt was tested empty. The event log shows that test run at 17:36, with the first item after the test entering the belt at 17:52 according to the photo-eye counter.

Ramp supervisor Teodric Vanhallow was at the loading end of the belt when it stopped and reported the stoppage to the control room by radio. He assigned six handlers and one electric tug to move oversize items to the aircraft holds, and he reported that the tug battery had to be swapped once during the afternoon. Handlers hand-carried oversize items to aircraft between 14:08 and 17:52. The count of hand-carried items differs between two accounts, with 38 items in the station manager's report and 46 items in the check-in agent's account. At the check-in hatch beside desks 14 to 16, passengers carrying surfboards and cello cases were asked to wait while handlers were summoned. Airline station manager Ysolde Brackwith reported that two departures were held for ten minutes each to complete loading, and her report notes that a pram and a wheelchair frame were tagged for gate delivery rather than the hold.

The sources disagree on the cause of the overload trip. The maintenance work order attributes it solely to the worn drive coupling seizing under normal load. The ramp supervisor's statement attributes it solely to an overlong rolled carpet bag wedging at the transfer point, with the coupling wearing only as a result. This discrepancy should be resolved before corrective actions are finalised.

Sources: Airline station manager Ysolde Brackwith's report, Skellmark Harbour Airport Oversize Belt Photo-Eye Counter, Skellmark Harbour Airport Maintenance Work Order, Ramp supervisor Teodric Vanhallow's statement, Skellmark Harbour Airport Oversize Belt Event Log, Check-in desk agent Lorcan Pellerby's account

The reclaim carousels in the Hollowmere Regional Airport arrivals hall stopped during the evening arrivals bank on a Friday. Ground handler Pavel Ostrowe was driving a tug with four loaded carts toward the Tollbrook Apron bay when that instruction was issued. Handlers kept the loaded carts in rows grouped by flight, and held bags were stacked on the open apron outside the cart bay until the carousels were restored. Carousels 1 and 3 restarted at 21:05 and Carousel 2 at 21:40. Incident Report: Controlled Release from Perrin Mere, Stillwater Narrows Dam, 17 February

At 9:50 a.m. on 17 February, a controlled release began through the number 1 sluice spillway gate at Stillwater Narrows Dam. According to the dam authority's release notice, the release was ordered to lower Perrin Mere ahead of a scheduled inspection of the intake tower, with the gate to remain open until the lake had fallen by 0.6 metres. Gate operator Hallam Rooke raised the gate in two stages, first to a quarter opening and then to a half opening, and recorded a loud, steady roar from the stilling basin once it reached half opening. The gate was closed that afternoon after the target lake level was met.

Public notification and access measures were in place before the release. A warning notice was posted at the Ostlewick footpath stile about 40 minutes before the gate opened, and volunteers with the footpath patrol closed the lower footpath with tape at both ends of the riverside section. Two walkers turned back at the tape and used the road instead.

Downstream effects were significant. At the sonde station 3.2 kilometres below the dam, beside the Ostlewick footbridge, the river peak is recorded differently across sources: 1.8 metres above normal in the sonde station record and 2.3 metres in the gate operator's statement. Turbidity rose sharply soon after the water arrived, and river temperature dropped by about 2 degrees Celsius as colder lake water came through. Edda Marnock, the parish allotment warden, observed river water spilling over the lowest allotment path and into nearby plots, and rising water carried away wheelbarrows. The patrol notebook records eleven wheelbarrows lost, while her own account records seven. She walked the allotment boundary and asked plot holders to move tools and compost bins away from the bank.

The Perrin Mere inflow gauge showed inflow steady at about 6 cubic metres per second throughout the morning, indicating the drawdown was driven by the release rather than any upstream change. The discrepancies in peak water level and wheelbarrow counts should be reconciled before the incident is closed.

Sources: Ostlewick Footpath Volunteer Patrol Notebook, Stillwater Narrows Dam Authority Release Notice, Ostlewick Parish Allotment Warden Edda Marnock's account, Cobbet River Sonde Station Record, Stillwater Narrows Dam Gate Operator Hallam Rooke's statement, Perrin Mere Inflow Gauge Record

The tilt-tray sorter at Pennywhistle Strand Airport stopped at 08:17 on a Saturday and did not resume automated sorting until late morning. The controller recorded the stop as a jam-detect trip at the merge between the induction loop and the main sorter loop. Maintenance technician Ludovica Strand-Aske reached the merge platform at 08:34 after the area was made safe and locked out, and she reported finding two trays at the merge. Her work report attributes the jam solely to worn tray bearings that left two trays sitting unevenly, independent of any bag. Baggage handler Idris Calderwood, however, described a soft-sided bag with a loose strap snagging at the merge and wedging between trays. The accounts therefore disagree on the cause, and the operations team should resolve this before drawing conclusions.

Check-in desks were instructed at 08:25 to keep accepting bags and to hold them in the back-of-house queue. Check-in supervisor Bram Tollervey recorded that the queue at the desks' belt end grew past the marked limit line at about 08:40, and that the desks resumed sending bags onto the belt at 11:10. The fully held queue was cleared at 12:05 according to Tollervey's notes, while the ground operations log gives 11:40. The photo-eye record shows the merge beam clear again at 08:36, and a photo-eye at the merge point remained blocked continuously for 14 seconds before the trip was recorded.

The controller log shows the loop was restarted in manual jog mode at 10:48 and returned to full automatic sorting at 11:05. Calderwood stated that the aisle beside the make-up carousel was crowded with staff pushing carts during the outage. The ground operations log records that 11 departures were scheduled to close check-in between 08:30 and 10:30, that two flights departed later than scheduled, and that the longest delay was 35 minutes. It also notes that a ski-equipment group was among that morning's passengers, with oversized items taken to a separate hatch.

Sources: Induction Zone Photo-Eye Record, Check-in supervisor Bram Tollervey's notes, Sorter Controller Event Log, Maintenance technician Ludovica Strand-Aske's work report, Baggage handler Idris Calderwood's statement, Pennywhistle Strand Airport Ground Operations Log

At 06:42 on a Tuesday, the main outbound sortation line at Corvane Island Airport stopped after an emergency stop was logged on the main sortation loop at 06:42:17. Automated sorting did not resume until the loop was restarted at 13:05. During the outage, baggage hall shift supervisor Ines Okafor-Lund, who was supervising a crew of nine, asked the terminal duty manager to pause new check-in bag acceptance for a short period, and two additional handlers were brought in from the cargo shed.

With the loop halted, handlers carried bags by hand from the check-in belts to the aircraft carts. Reyes recalls the hand-carrying area filling with suitcases stacked two or three high along the wall. The Operations Log notes that the first Skerrin Air departure was held while bags were matched to passengers. The Skerrin Air Departure Control Record shows three departures scheduled between 07:15 and 09:00 that morning. The first flight's delay is recorded in minutes rather than hours, and the last affected departure is listed as leaving after the loop was restored.

The cause of the stop is reported inconsistently. Ines Okafor-Lund states that an oversized bag struck the loop's guard rail and tripped the safety circuit. Maintenance technician Halvard Quist states that the diverter arm jammed at the third merge point. Quist reached the sorter hall within about fifteen minutes of being called, found a diverter arm near the third merge point, and reported that the pneumatic fitting on the arm was warm to the touch. The Sorter Control System Event Record shows drive motor current dropped to zero at the moment of the stop. Because the two accounts identify different causes, the root cause should be confirmed before the incident is closed.

Sources: Corvane Island Airport Operations Log, Halvard Quist, Ines Okafor-Lund, Skerrin Air Departure Control Record, Sorter Control System Event Record, Tamsin Reyes

The Stillwater Narrows Dam released water from Perrin Mere into the Cobbet River on 17 February, beginning at 9:50 a.m. The release was ordered to lower the lake ahead of a scheduled inspection of the intake tower, and the release notice specified that the number 1 sluice spillway gate would stay open until the lake had fallen by 0.6 metres. Gate operator Hallam Rooke raised the gate in two stages, first to a quarter opening and then to a half opening, and reported a loud, steady roar from the stilling basin once the gate reached half opening. The gate was closed the same afternoon after the target lake level was reached.

Downstream effects were recorded at the sonde station beside the Ostlewick footbridge, 3.2 kilometres below the dam. Accounts differ on the peak water level, with one record giving 1.8 metres above normal and another giving 2.3 metres. The station logged a sharp rise in turbidity shortly after the water arrived and a drop in river temperature of about 2 degrees Celsius as colder lake water reached the reach. Volunteers closed the lower footpath with tape at both ends of the riverside section, and a warning notice was posted at the Ostlewick footpath stile roughly 40 minutes before the gate opened. Two walkers turned back at the tape and used the road instead. Allotment warden Edda Marnock reported river water spilling over the lowest allotment path and into the plots nearest the bank, and she advised plot holders to move tools and compost bins away from the riverbank. Wheelbarrows were carried off the lowest allotment path by the rising water, with the patrol notebook recording eleven and Marnock's account recording seven, a discrepancy the team should reconcile. The Perrin Mere inflow gauge shows steady inflow of about 6 cubic metres per second through the morning, indicating that the drawdown was driven by the release rather than any change in inflow.

On 17 February, a controlled release was made from Stillwater Narrows Dam when the number 1 sluice spillway gate was opened at 9:50 a.m. to draw down Perrin Mere ahead of a scheduled inspection of the intake tower. The release notice specified that the gate would remain open until the lake level fell by 0.6 metres. Gate operator Hallam Rooke raised the gate in two stages, first to a quarter opening and then to a half opening, and recorded a loud, steady roar from the stilling basin once it reached half opening. The gate was lowered to closed the same afternoon after the target lake level was reached.

The Perrin Mere inflow gauge recorded inflow steady at about 6 cubic metres per second through the morning, indicating that the lake drawdown resulted from the release rather than any change in incoming water. Downstream, the sonde station beside the Ostlewick footbridge, 3.2 kilometres below the dam, logged a river peak 1.8 metres above normal in one record and 2.3 metres in another. Turbidity rose sharply soon after the water arrived, and river temperature dropped by about 2 degrees Celsius as colder lake water passed through.

Local precautions were taken on the ground. A warning notice was posted at the Ostlewick footpath stile about 40 minutes before the gate opened. Volunteers closed the lower footpath with tape at both ends of the riverside section, and two walkers turned back and used the road instead. Allotment warden Edda Marnock observed river water spilling over the lowest allotment path and into the plots nearest the bank, inspected the boundary, and instructed plot holders to move tools and compost bins away from the riverbank. Accounts of losses differ: the patrol notebook reports seven wheelbarrows carried off the lowest path by the rising water, while Marnock's account reports eleven.

The Stillwater Narrows Dam released water from Perrin Mere into the Cobbet River on 17 February, starting at 9:50 a.m. The release was ordered to lower the lake ahead of a scheduled inspection of the intake tower. The release notice specified that the number 1 sluice spillway gate would remain open until the lake had fallen by 0.6 metres. Gate operator Hallam Rooke raised the gate in two stages, first to a quarter opening and then to a half opening, and reported a loud, steady roar from the stilling basin once the gate reached half opening. The gate was closed the same afternoon after the target lake level was reached.

Downstream effects were recorded at the sonde station beside the Ostlewick footbridge, 3.2 kilometres below the dam. Accounts differ on the peak water level, with one record giving 1.8 metres above normal and another giving 2.3 metres. The station logged a sharp rise in turbidity shortly after the water arrived and a drop in river temperature of about 2 degrees Celsius as colder lake water reached the reach. Volunteers closed the lower footpath with tape at both ends of the riverside section, and a warning notice was posted at the Ostlewick footpath stile roughly 40 minutes before the gate opened. Two walkers turned back at the tape and used the road instead.

Allotment warden Edda Marnock reported river water spilling over the lowest allotment path and into the plots nearest the bank, and she advised plot holders to move tools and compost bins away from the riverbank. Wheelbarrows were carried off the lowest allotment path by the rising water. The patrol notebook recorded eleven wheelbarrows, while Marnock's account recorded seven, a discrepancy the team should reconcile. The Perrin Mere inflow gauge shows steady inflow of about 6 cubic metres per second through the morning, indicating that the drawdown was driven by the release rather than any change in inflow.

Sources: Ostlewick Footpath Volunteer Patrol Notebook, Stillwater Narrows Dam Authority Release Notice, Ostlewick Parish Allotment Warden Edda Marnock's account, Cobbet River Sonde Station Record, Stillwater Narrows Dam Gate Operator Hallam Rooke's statement, Perrin Mere Inflow Gauge Record

On a January morning at about 4:40 a.m., a gas leak was detected at Pellam Bakery on Calloway Row in Wexmoor, leading to the evacuation of the bakery, Soltan Optical, and a laundromat called Brightwash. The first alert came from the fixed methane detector on the bakery's loading dock wall, which alarmed when its reading passed 20 percent of the lower explosive limit. Night supervisor Odalys Brennt was mixing dough in the back room when she heard the siren and smelled sulfur near the dock door. Before leaving, she shut off the ovens' gas supply at the main bakery valve. The Calloway Row Gas Co. dispatch record logged the call as an emergency odor report. Wexmoor Fire and Rescue responded with one engine and one command vehicle. The fire incident log places the engine's arrival at 4:49 a.m., while Brennt's account gives 4:58 a.m. Firefighters closed Calloway Row to traffic between Dunmere Street and Hask Lane.

Gas utility field technician Tamsin Fordyce arrived with a combustible gas indicator and measured readings along the foundation wall beside the loading dock. She shut off the service line at the curb valve outside the bakery, after which the detector's log shows readings falling below the alarm threshold. Her excavation found that the buried steel service line, installed in 1974 according to the dispatch record, had a pinhole opening where the coating had worn away and rust had penetrated. The detector's peak recorded value was 47 percent of the lower explosive limit. Gas service to the bakery was off for roughly six to nine hours before restoration, though the dispatch record and Brennt give different durations.

Imre Soltan, owner of Soltan Optical, was called by police at his home. He arrived to find his shop's front windows fogged with cold and the street lit by emergency lights. He lost a morning of appointments and posted a notice telling customers to return the next day.

The Stillwater Narrows Dam opened its number 1 sluice spillway gate at 9:50 a.m. on 17 February to lower Perrin Mere into the Cobbet River, ahead of a scheduled inspection of the intake tower. The release notice specified that the gate was to remain open until the lake had fallen by 0.6 metres. Gate operator Hallam Rooke raised the gate in two stages, to a quarter opening and then to a half opening, and reported a loud, steady roar from the stilling basin once it reached half opening. A warning notice was posted at the Ostlewick footpath stile roughly 40 minutes before the gate opened. Volunteers from the footpath patrol then taped off both ends of the lower riverside footpath, and two walkers turned back and used the road instead.

Allotment warden Edda Marnock observed river water spilling over the lowest allotment path and into the nearest plots. She advised plot holders to move tools and compost bins away from the riverbank. The patrol records that rising water carried away eleven wheelbarrows from the lowest allotment path, whereas Marnock's account gives seven. This discrepancy needs confirmation before the figure is finalised.

Downstream, the Cobbet River sonde station, 3.2 kilometres below the dam beside the Ostlewick footbridge, logged a peak of 1.8 metres above normal level. Turbidity rose sharply and river temperature fell by about 2 degrees Celsius as colder lake water arrived. Hallam Rooke's statement gives a peak of 2.3 metres, which differs from the station record and must be reconciled. The gate was closed the same afternoon once the target lake level was reached. Gauge records show Perrin Mere inflow steady at about 6 cubic metres per second throughout the morning.

Tamsin Fordyce, a gas utility field technician, arrived with a combustible gas indicator and took readings along the foundation wall beside the loading dock. She shut off the service line at the curb valve outside the bakery and found that the buried steel line, dating from 1974 according to the dispatch record, had a pinhole opening where the coating had worn away and rust had eaten through. The detector log shows readings falling below the alarm threshold after the curb valve was closed.

Gas service to the bakery was interrupted for roughly six to nine hours before restoration. The dispatch record indicates about six hours, while Brennt's account indicates about nine; this difference also requires reconciliation. Imre Soltan, owner of Soltan Optical, was called by police at his home and arrived to find the shop's front windows fogged with cold and the street lit by emergency lights. His shop lost a morning of appointments, and he posted a notice directing customers to return the following day.

On a Sunday evening in October, at approximately 9:15 p.m., the fixed gas detector in the boiler room at Fenwick Hill Care Home registered gas at 12 percent of the lower explosive limit. The reading rose over the following minutes and peaked at 38 percent of the lower explosive limit. The detector's alarm relay sounded the building alarm once the reading passed 20 percent. The night charge nurse, Imelda Torvaldsen, detected a rotten-egg odor near the basement stairwell while carrying linen and placed the emergency gas call from the care home's staff phone, which Tarnby Gas Network logged as the first emergency report. Before leaving, she closed the basement fire door and switched off the kitchen's gas appliances.

Staff evacuated 34 residents, many using wheelchairs or walking frames, to St. Odran's Church Hall two blocks away. The timing of the final resident's arrival differs between sources: the nurse's account places it at about 9:50 p.m., while the maintenance log records about 10:20 p.m. This discrepancy needs to be reconciled during review. Volunteers and two off-duty carers provided blankets and hot drinks at the hall.

Network engineer Basil Okonkwo-Reyes arrived from a depot about six kilometers away, checked the basement with a handheld combustible gas meter, and closed the meter isolation valve in the street-side cabinet to stop supply to the building. The cause remains disputed. The engineer attributed the leak to a worn flexible hose connector, whereas the network's incident report attributes it to a faulty gas valve inside the boiler, with the hose connector found sound. No residents or staff required hospital treatment. Gas service was restored the following afternoon after pressure testing of the pipework. The boiler, a floor-standing unit installed about eleven years earlier, was last serviced in March of the same year.

Sources: Tarnby Gas Network incident report, Nurse Imelda Torvaldsen (night charge nurse), Technician Basil Okonkwo-Reyes (Tarnby Gas Network engineer), Fenwick Hill Care Home maintenance log, Boiler room fixed gas detector record

Incident Report: Suspected Gas Leak, Sallowmere Ferry Terminal Canteen, Kelderwick

On a Saturday in March, shortly after 2:10 p.m., a suspected gas leak was identified in the basement kitchen of the Sallowmere Ferry Terminal canteen. Canteen supervisor Imogen Draycott first noticed a strong rotten-egg odour near the walk-in pantry while preparing sandwich trays. She reported that the canteen's gas range had been serviced in February. Before leaving, she switched off the kitchen's electric fryers and directed the three kitchen staff to exit through the service stairwell. The fire service was called from the terminal at 2:16 p.m., and two engines were dispatched. Firefighters entered the basement to check the kitchen. Accounts differ on crew size: the dispatch record indicates two crews of two, while another account describes a single crew of three.

Terminal safety officer Osric Valbane carried portable gas detector unit KH-7 into the basement corridor and took readings outside the kitchen door. The unit recorded a peak of 38 percent of the lower explosive limit in the corridor, above its alarm threshold of 20 percent. Its last logged corridor measurement showed readings below 5 percent. Once the engines arrived, Valbane closed the terminal's main gas isolation valve in the plant room. The harbour authority log records that the ground-floor ticket hall was cleared of staff and visitors.

Boarding for the 2:45 p.m. sailing to Ormsey Island was suspended. Deck purser Tamsin Rooke stopped passengers at the gangway and directed them to the car park beside the fish market, including about a dozen passengers with bicycles who had to be moved away from the quay entrance. Accounts of the suspension length differ: the harbour authority log states about 50 minutes, while Rooke recorded about 90 minutes. The delayed sailing eventually departed with passengers aboard.

Sources: Tamsin Rooke, Kelderwick Harbour Authority Incident Log, Imogen Draycott, Kelderwick Fire Service Dispatch Record, Osric Valbane, Portable gas detector unit KH-7 readout

At approximately 4:40 a.m. on a January morning, a gas leak was detected at Pellam Bakery on Calloway Row in Wexmoor, resulting in the evacuation of three businesses: Pellam Bakery, Soltan Optical, and the Brightwash laundromat. The detector log shows readings falling below the alarm threshold after the curb valve was closed. The Calloway Row Gas Co. dispatch record logs the call as an emergency odor report. Gas service to the bakery was off for roughly six hours according to the dispatch record and about nine hours according to Brennt's account, a difference that also needs to be resolved.

Imre Soltan, owner of Soltan Optical, was contacted at home by police and found his shop's front windows fogged and the street lit by emergency lights. He lost a morning of appointments and posted a notice directing customers to return the following day.

The oversize baggage belt at Skellmark Harbour Airport stopped at 14:08 on a Wednesday afternoon after the belt controller logged an overload trip on the transfer conveyor drive. The belt did not return to automatic mode until 17:44. The photo-eye counter recorded no items entering the belt during the outage. The event log shows the belt was run empty for test at 17:36 following a relay reset, and the first item after that test entered the belt at 17:52. While the belt was down, the oversize drop-off hatch beside check-in desks 14 to 16 could not accept items, and passengers carrying surfboards and cello cases were asked to wait at the hatch while handlers were summoned.

Ramp supervisor Teodric Vanhallow was at the loading end of the belt when it stopped and notified the control room by radio. He assigned six handlers and one electric tug to move oversize items to the aircraft holds, and reported that the tug battery was swapped once during the afternoon. Handlers hand-carried oversize items to aircraft between 14:08 and 17:52. The reported count of affected items varies by account: the station manager's report cites 38 items, while the check-in agent's account cites 46. Airline station manager Ysolde Brackwith reported that two departures were held for ten minutes each to complete loading, and her report notes that a pram and a wheelchair frame were tagged for gate delivery rather than the hold.

A maintenance technician opened the transfer conveyor guard at 14:31 and found the drive coupling hot to the touch. The work order records that a replacement drive coupling was fitted and the overload relay reset before the belt was tested empty. The cause of the trip is attributed differently across sources. The maintenance work order states the overload was caused solely by the worn drive coupling seizing under normal load, while Vanhallow's statement attributes it solely to an overlong rolled carpet bag wedging at the transfer point, with the coupling wearing only as a result. The operations team should reconcile these accounts before closing the review.

Sources: Airline station manager Ysolde Brackwith's report, Skellmark Harbour Airport Oversize Belt Photo-Eye Counter, Skellmark Harbour Airport Maintenance Work Order, Ramp supervisor Teodric Vanhallow's statement, Skellmark Harbour Airport Oversize Belt Event Log, Check-in desk agent Lorcan Pellerby's account

At the time, a children's story session with about 20 attendees was underway on the ground floor. Facilities engineer Marcus Delacroix-Boyne closed the main gas valve at the boiler closet, and the laminator and two large-format plotters in the print room were switched off at the wall.

The detector had been installed fourteen months earlier and had passed its most recent calibration check. The room was ventilated, and readings had fallen below 1 percent of the lower explosive limit by 5:10 p.m. A corroded section of service pipe was later found beneath the print room floor, which appears to be the source of the leak.

The following report covers a gas leak detected at approximately 4:40 a.m. on a January morning at Pellam Bakery on Calloway Row in Wexmoor, which led to the evacuation of three businesses: Pellam Bakery, Soltan Optical, and a laundromat called Brightwash. The detector log shows readings dropping below the alarm threshold after the valve was closed. Fordyce found that the buried steel service line, which the dispatch record lists as installed in 1974, had a pinhole opening where the coating had worn away and rust had penetrated the pipe.

Imre Soltan, owner of Soltan Optical, was contacted by police at his home and found his shop's front windows fogged with cold. He lost a morning of appointments and posted a notice directing customers to return the following day. Operations should review the service line's age and corrosion history, confirm the restoration timeline, and assess the notification and business-impact process for the evacuated tenants.

Gas utility field technician Tamsin Fordyce arrived with a combustible gas indicator and measured readings along the foundation wall beside the loading dock. She shut off the service line at the curb valve outside the bakery, after which the detector's log shows readings falling below the alarm threshold. Incident Summary: Gas Leak, Hollin Vale Public Library

On a Wednesday afternoon in November, the fixed methane detector in the lower-level print room registered a rise in readings, reaching 0.6 percent of the lower explosive limit at approximately 3:25 p.m. The detector peaked at 9 percent of the lower explosive limit at 3:41 p.m. Reading room attendant Odile Prewitt detected a sulfur-like odor near the stairwell while shelving returned picture books and reported it to the front desk before the alarm had finished sounding. A children's story session with about 20 attendees was underway on the ground floor at the time. The incident report records eleven attendees as children under ten, while Prewitt's account gives fourteen. This discrepancy must be reconciled before the review is finalized.

Staff evacuated the building through the front doors shortly after the alarm, and all evacuated persons gathered in the car park on Tannery Lane. Facilities engineer Marcus Delacroix-Boyne closed the main gas valve at the boiler closet and switched off the laminator and two large-format plotters in the print room. Thessaly Gas Emergency Dispatch logged the call from the front desk at 3:29 p.m. and assigned a crew as a priority response. The detector had been installed fourteen months earlier and had passed its most recent calibration check.

Readings fell below 1 percent of the lower explosive limit by 5:10 p.m. following ventilation of the room. A corroded section of service pipe was subsequently identified beneath the print room floor. The library remained closed to the public for the remainder of the day. Accounts differ on the length of closure, which is reported as roughly 20 to 26 hours, with reopening at either 11:30 a.m. or 5:30 p.m. the following day. This variance must also be resolved before the review is finalized.

Sources: Reading room attendant Odile Prewitt, Fixed methane detector log (Unit R-2), Hollin Vale Library Incident Report, Facilities engineer Marcus Delacroix-Boyne, Thessaly Gas Emergency Dispatch Record

The incident began on the night of 9 March, when a chilled-water pipe above the server room at Pellam Row Credit Cooperative burst. The building management system log shows chilled-water loop pressure falling from 4.1 bar to 1.3 bar within six minutes. The building called the Halvard Fire and Rescue dispatch line at 02:19. Water reached a depth of about 9 centimetres under the raised floor before pumping began, and three of the room's eighteen racks held storage arrays whose lower shelves were submerged.

Database administrator Ines Okafor, logging in remotely, began moving the primary database to the backup site at Corrow Park. Member-account services were fully unavailable during the shutdown, and mobile banking and card authorization were also unavailable to members. Accounts of the outage duration differ. The database administrator reports about 95 minutes before the backup site took over, while the facility incident report gives about 3 hours. The backup site took over member-account services in the early morning, though at reduced speed.

The cause of the pipe failure is also disputed. The facility incident report attributes the burst solely to a corroded coupling failing, with nothing else contributing. Ms Brandvold attributes it solely to a pressure surge from a faulty pump valve, not corrosion. The operations team should resolve this conflict before closing the review, as it determines which remediation applies.

She found the door seal damp while the floor near the entrance remained dry, and she placed plastic sheeting over two server cabinets before the shutdown began. By the end of the shutdown, five cabinets had water on them. Two on-call engineers were contacted at home and reached the building. Contractor Dillon Aversley located a blocked condensate drain line on the roof beside the chiller plant, cleared it with a drain rod, and flushed it with a hose. He also recorded that the stained ceiling tile above row 4 had sagged by about 6 centimetres. The facilities log notes that the rooftop chiller plant had been running at full load during a heat spell that week.

Customs brokers were instructed to submit manual paper declarations until the servers returned to service. A discrepancy exists in the cabinet count: Aversley's job report indicates three cabinets had water on them by the end of the shutdown, whereas Fairweather's count is five. This discrepancy should be reconciled before the incident is closed.

The leak sensor alarm was acknowledged from the facilities desk, and two on-call engineers were contacted at home and attended the building.

Contractor Dillon Aversley located a blocked condensate drain line on the roof beside the chiller plant, cleared it with a drain rod, and flushed it with a hose. His report also notes that the stained ceiling tile above row 4 had sagged by approximately 6 centimetres. The facilities log indicates that the rooftop chiller plant had been operating at full load during a heat spell that week. Customs brokers were instructed to submit manual paper declarations until the servers were restored.

The conflicting shutdown order should be resolved before root-cause conclusions are finalised.

Duty officer Rhona Fairweather, walking the corridor outside the room, observed water dripping onto the cold-aisle containment panels. On first inspection, the door seal was damp but the floor near the entrance remained dry. Before the shutdown began, she covered two server cabinets with plastic sheeting. By the end of the shutdown, five server cabinets had water on them.

Power to the room's power distribution unit was lost at 23:41 according to the facilities log, while the uninterruptible power supply event log records the loss at 23:48. The unit switched to battery power at that point, showing a runtime estimate of 22 minutes at switchover. The battery was drained to its low-charge warning level before the unit was turned off. Two on-call engineers were contacted at home and attended the building. The facilities log notes that the rooftop chiller plant had been running at full load during a heat spell that week.

Contractor Dillon Aversley located a blocked condensate drain line on the roof beside the chiller plant and cleared it with a drain rod before flushing it with a hose. His report records that the stained ceiling tile above row 4 had sagged by about 6 centimetres. Customs brokers were instructed to submit manual paper declarations until the servers were restored.

Sources: Contractor Dillon Aversley's job report, Duty officer Rhona Fairweather's statement, Marsden Quay Customs Facilities Log, Server Room Under-Floor Leak Sensor Record, Uninterruptible Power Supply Event Log

On the night of 17 June, a water leak through the ceiling of the third-floor server room at the Marsden Quay Port Customs Authority led to the shutdown of the cargo-clearance servers. Duty officer Rhona Fairweather noticed drips falling onto the cold-aisle containment panels while walking the corridor outside the room. When she first looked in, the door seal was damp but the floor near the entrance was still dry. Before the shutdown began, she placed plastic sheeting over two server cabinets. By the end of the shutdown, five server cabinets had water on them.

The under-floor leak sensor first reported moisture in zone B of the raised floor and logged moisture in zone C eleven minutes later. Its alarm output was acknowledged from the facilities desk. The feed to the room's power distribution unit was lost at 23:41 according to the facilities log, although the uninterruptible power supply event log records the loss at 23:48. The uninterruptible power supply then switched to battery power, showing a 22-minute runtime estimate at switchover, and the battery was drained to its low-charge warning level before the unit was turned off.

Contractor Dillon Aversley found a blocked condensate drain line on the roof beside the chiller plant, which was cleared with a drain rod and flushed with a hose. He recorded that the stained ceiling tile above row 4 had sagged by about 6 centimetres, and three server cabinets had water on them by the end of the shutdown. The facilities log notes that the rooftop chiller plant had been running at full load during a heat spell that week. Two on-call engineers reached the building after being phoned at home, and customs brokers were told to submit manual paper declarations until the servers returned.

Sources: Contractor Dillon Aversley's job report, Duty officer Rhona Fairweather's statement, Marsden Quay Customs Facilities Log, Server Room Under-Floor Leak Sensor Record, Uninterruptible Power Supply Event Log
